en: The Yoga Mahātantrarāja Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Censor of the Third Rank, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, Subject Fa-xian, by Imperial Decree.
1. The Introduction, Chapter One. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-Vajra, was dwelling within the great celestial palace in the Heaven of Pure Light (*Śuddhāvāsakāyika*). That palace was adorned with various jewels; its pillars were made of pure, exquisite vajra-gems, and its vajra-bells, stirred by a gentle breeze, produced subtle and wondrous sounds. Furthermore, it was arrayed with various sublime offerings and decorated with the precious vajra-wheel and other such treasures.

These are formed through the various transformations of the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, and extend even to all Buddhas born from the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata, namely: Akṣobhya Buddha, Ratnasambhava Buddha, Amitāyus Buddha, Amoghasiddhi Buddha, and so forth.

Furthermore, from the gates on the four sides, there emerge hosts of bodhisattvas and various holy sages and wrathful vidyārājas, along with countless retinues such as Citta-Citi, Natta-Nati, Kinkara-Kinkari, and others.
That Buddha dwells securely in samādhi, never abandoning great wisdom, great kindness, and great compassion, and exerts great diligence to rescue and deliver sentient beings.

Within that assembly, there are also countless retinues of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, surrounding the World-Honored One, the Great All-Illuminating Vajra Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having looked upon the Great Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi within the assembly, emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire gathering; the light then returned and re-entered the Buddha’s body.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and with leaping joy gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance. Throwing down his vajra, he knelt with his right knee on the ground and, joining his palms in reverent salutation, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"By what cause and by what condition has this great radiance been emitted?"
"The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not emit rays of light without cause or condition; yet now, seeing this light, we in this great assembly are all struck with wonder and astonishment.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will roar the lion’s roar and proclaim it for our sake."

At that time, having accepted the request of Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, the World-Honored One entered a great samādhi called the Great King of Teachings on the Yoga of the Transformation of Great Wisdom. Among all teachings, it is the most supreme and most honored; the rites performed therein are not difficult to accomplish.
This is the Vajrajñāna-mahāsukhopāya-sarvatattvagarbha, which skillfully accomplishes the supreme wisdom-upāya, the Mahāsukha-vajra, and the Mahānirmāṇa-vajra-samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having emerged from samādhi, expounded the Yoga Mahātantrarāja Sūtra, including the Samaya Maṇḍala and various dharmas, namely:

the dharma of painted images, the dharma of visualization, the dharma of recitation, the dharma of performing wrathful rites and glances, the dharma of samādhi, the dharma of summoning, the dharma of subjugation, the dharma of striking evil māras, the dharma of fixed dates, the dharma of illness, the dharma of feverish affliction, the dharma of accomplishing tasks, the ultimate dharma, the dharma of empowerment, the dharma of the characteristics of the ācārya, and the dharma of receiving disciples. "I shall now explain these various secret teachings; you all should listen with single-minded devotion."
At that time, all those Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the entire assembly, received the instruction and listened.
Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"First, one must draw near to the ācārya; Then all dharmas to be performed can be accomplished."
If one does not attend upon an ācārya, the various dharmas one practices cannot be accomplished.
I shall now describe the virtues of that ācārya;
you bodhisattvas and the entire assembly should listen with a sincere mind and respectfully honor his discipline and great wisdom.
Patient, pure, upright, and free from indolence, Skilled in understanding secret mantras and their applications,
As well as the rituals for powder altars and their procedural rules, One is able to comprehend the ten kinds of ultimate meanings.
Bestowing constant fearlessness upon all sentient beings, Ever delighting in the secret Dharma of the Mahāyāna,
Fully able to comprehend all non-Buddhist teachings, They uphold the precepts, practice cultivation, and possess the Vinaya.
One who has mastered the profound Mahāyāna teachings and is able to encompass the secret, ultimate meaning—
if they can fully possess the aforementioned ritual methods— for this reason they are called an Ācārya.
If one acts for the benefit of others without compassion, lacks right faith due to indolence,
violates the precepts, is distracted, and lacks self-restraint, one will slander the teachings upon seeing or hearing them.
Thus, one who is foolish, evil, and devoid of roots of virtue is unfit to act as a teacher for the practice of the Dharma;
if one possesses the ritual characteristics and methods described above, they should serve as the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) for the disciple.
This powder altar may serve as the master (ācārya);
it shall instruct in all the teachings and dharmas, and all the secret mantras (mantra) spoken therein shall be accomplished. The disciple, possessing such virtues, is likewise so.
Always delighting in the subtle and wondrous Dharma of meditative concentration, reverently honoring and being filial toward the ācārya,
and constantly making offerings to all the worthy and holy ones—
how does one serve the ācārya?
Seeing all Buddhas as equal and without distinction, one should always regard the Vajrācārya as the Great Tathāgata Ratnasambhava; such is the Ācārya, an ocean of great wisdom.
Bestowing great wealth as if from a wish-fulfilling jewel, One should always praise the great virtues of the ācārya;
Do not look for faults or engage in slander, For by honoring them in this way, one attains the realization of the Dharma.

If one acts with unlawful contempt and ultimately refuses to comply, or if a person should step upon the shadow of their teacher, that person commits a sin no different from destroying a stupa; all that they do and all that they seek shall remain unfulfilled.
All Buddhas and noble sages forbid it; do not slander the ācārya, even in your dreams.
Such people of evil karma and delusion will constantly be startled and tormented by various māras.
The wise should always keep themselves far removed from this.
As for the hells such as Avīci that have been described—once one falls into those hells, there is no time of emergence; this is the fruit obtained by slandering an ācārya.

Therefore, with a sincere mind, seek enlightenment; Make offerings to and serve the ācārya, Always being respectful, honoring, and filial toward them, For this can bestow the inconceivable, most supreme fruit.

Chapter Two: The Maṇḍala. From the *Buddhabhāṣita-yogamahātantrarāja-sūtra*, Chapter Two, the Maṇḍala. At that time, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, having surveyed the assembled multitude, entered the samādhi of the supreme secret vajra of the transformations of the wisdom of Great Yoga. Emerging from that concentration, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi:
"Listen now attentively, Vajrapāṇi!"

This King of Great Yoga Tantras—the King of Great Maṇḍalas, the most supreme and most honored among all maṇḍalas—is named the Vajra Capable of Accomplishment, the Treasury of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who receives empowerment within this maṇḍala, that person shall receive the empowerment rites of all maṇḍalas.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
“If there is anyone who beholds the five-colored powders within this maṇḍala, that person shall attain the honor and offerings due to all Tathāgatas.”

Furthermore, if there should be anyone who enters this maṇḍala, that person will be as if entering the buddha-fields of all the Tathāgatas and shall receive from all the Tathāgatas the prophecy of attaining buddhahood.

At that time, the ācārya first employs the rite of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) to protect himself according to the ritual rules, and adorns his body with all manner of ornaments. Thereafter, visualizing himself as the Wrathful Vidyārāja, he brandishes a vajra with his right hand and rings a vajra-bell with his left. Taking the vajra-steps, he circumambulates the site of the maṇḍala while reciting the syllable *HŪṂ*.
Then he proclaims: "I now dispatch all demons, including devas, humans, and asuras."
Having spoken thus, he again visualizes his own body as the Wrathful Vidyārāja and recites this mantra:

At that time, once the ācārya has performed each of these successive postures of walking and sitting, he shall employ the Immeasurable Invincible Vidyārāja, the Great Powerful Vidyārāja, and others, and according to the ritual, drive stakes into the ground of the maṇḍala to bind the boundaries of the ten directions.
Having performed this, one should further visualize that the ground of the maṇḍala becomes a vajra-ground, pervasive and blazing.

Having visualized thus, the ācārya then utters his own name and recites the syllable *HŪṂ* together with it; this subtle syllable is the most supreme and most venerable among all teachings. Thereafter, he should pray to the Earth Goddess according to the ritual using the root mantra.
The mantra is:

*tadvidhi viṣa kṣubhitasarvabuddhanudayanātsarya-naya-viśi-śu bhumibhūramita-sujā sarvasiddhiprāmṛti-cchiri-taṃ maṇḍalākṣepa-kāmya-haṃ*. At that time, having recited this mantra three times, the ācārya, moving with a heart of utmost sincerity, again invoked all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
The mantra is:

*Samantāvalokite mune, karuṇāhitātman, bhūmiparigrahakāriye, sarvatra saha āgamaya.* At that time, having recited this mantra three times, the Ācārya shall, in the center of the maṇḍala ground, fashion a circular maṇḍala using fragrant ointment.

When constructing this maṇḍala, one should recite the mantra of the Great Wheel Vidyārāja; thereafter, invite all the Buddhas and noble sages, present various kinds of sublime offerings, and entreat the Buddhas to be filled with joy.
At that time, the ācārya exits from outside the maṇḍala and arises in the ten directions.

Thereafter, the disciple remains overnight and enters the maṇḍala; according to the ritual, he performs the protection rites, receives the consecration with scented water, and further applies fragrant ointment to his heart center.

Visualize a *karmavajra* within your heart; bind the protection cord upon your right hand; use a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) to clean your teeth; spread auspicious grass (*darbha*) upon the ground; having performed the consecration (*adhitiṣṭhati*), settle into your seat.

At that time, the ācārya and the disciple received the three refuges, repented of their karmic obstructions, dedicated the merit, and made aspirations. Even to the point where the disciple offered his body and life as alms and gave rise to the great bodhicitta, the ācārya then recited the gāthā of the three refuges:
"I now take refuge and pay homage to the Triple Gem. My Buddha has transcended the three realms of existence through vast eons;
The wondrous Dharma can eradicate the roots of affliction; The noble Saṅgha has attained sainthood and is honored for its freedom from desire."
All the sinful karmas I have committed in the past, I now repent with utmost sincerity before the Triple Gem;
Dedicating this merit for the benefit of all sentient beings, I vow to seek the realization of the fruit of Bodhi.

"When the disciple who has received the Dharma has recited this gāthā three times, the ācārya shall again instruct and expound the Dharma for the disciple according to his capacity and inclination, causing him to sincerely generate the great bodhicitta."
Thereafter, perform the offerings according to the ritual as before and dispatch the noble deities.
At that time, the disciple shall lie on his right side upon the ground of the maṇḍala; within his dream, he will certainly behold the visionary images.
On the second day, the Ācārya uses fresh, pure five-colored threads to mark out the maṇḍala.

At that time, the Ācārya visualizes that these threads are the true nature of the Dharmadhātu, the Universal Illumination Self-Nature King Tathāgata, who is the treasury of all Tathāgatas. Because the Dharmadhātu is pure, he is free from all defilements and is able to purify the realms of sentient beings; the five-colored powders used are the five Tathāgatas.

Having completed the visualization, the ācārya first scatters the colored powders; then he causes the disciple to perform the first boundary-binding (sīmābandha); thirdly, he bestows the three refuges upon the disciple; fourthly, he causes the disciple to enter the maṇḍala; and fifthly, he performs the rite of dismissal (visarjana).

That maṇḍala has three grades of measurement: the superior grade is one thousand cubits, the middling grade is five hundred cubits, and the inferior grade is five cubits down to two cubits or even one cubit. Its form is square, with four gates and four towers; in the center, an eight-spoked wheel is fashioned upon which the Tathāgata Samantaprabha is installed. To the east, Akṣobhya Buddha is placed; to the south, Ratnasambhava Buddha; to the west, Amitāyus Buddha; and to the north, Amoghasiddhi Buddha.
Furthermore, one should place four attendant bodhisattvas at the four corners of the wheel:

in the northeast corner, place the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā; in the southeast corner, place the Bodhisattva Māmakī; in the southwest corner, place the Bodhisattva Pāṇḍaravāsinī; and in the northwest corner, place the Bodhisattva Tārā.
Furthermore, in the second tier of the maṇḍala, one should place four bodhisattvas:
Sattvavajra Bodhisattva in the east, Ratnavajra Bodhisattva in the south, Dharmavajra Bodhisattva in the west, and Karmavajra Bodhisattva in the north.
Furthermore, one should place four bodhisattvas at the four corners of the maṇḍala:

in the northeast corner, place the Bodhisattva Cundā; in the southeast corner, place the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhā; in the southwest corner, place the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī; and in the northwest corner, place the Bodhisattva Vajrasaṃkhalā.
Furthermore, in the third tier of the maṇḍala, sixteen great bodhisattvas are installed.
In the eastern direction, four bodhisattvas are installed:
Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Gandhahasti Bodhisattva, and Jñānaketu Bodhisattva.
In the southern direction, one should install four bodhisattvas:
Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, and Bodhisattva Pratibhānakūṭa.
Furthermore, in the western direction, one should install four bodhisattvas:
[The Buddhas] Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Sarvapāpavināśana Bodhisattva, Sarvadaurmanasyāndhakāravidhamana Bodhisattva, and Jvalanaprabha Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, in the northern direction, one should place four bodhisattvas:
Candraprabha Bodhisattva, Amṛtaprabha Bodhisattva, Gaganagañja Bodhisattva, and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, one should place the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka at the eastern gate of the maṇḍala, the Vidyārāja Prajñāntaka at the southern gate, the Vidyārāja Padmāntaka at the western gate, and the Vidyārāja Vighnāntaka at the northern gate.
Furthermore, one should place the four Vidyārājas at the four corners:

the Vidyārāja Acala is placed in the northeast corner; the Vidyārāja Takkirāja is placed in the southeast corner; the Vidyārāja Nīlananda is placed in the southwest corner; and the Vidyārāja Mahābala is placed in the northwest corner.

Furthermore, at each of the four corners outside the outer maṇḍala, place a vajra. The first inner circle is to be drawn with white powder; the second tier of the maṇḍala is to be drawn with powders of three colors—yellow, white, and blue; and the third tier of the maṇḍala is to be drawn with powders of five colors.
Having thus constructed the great maṇḍala, one should subsequently confer the empowerment ritual upon the disciples.

Furthermore, one should separately construct a two-tiered maṇḍala with four gates on its four sides. In the center, draw an eight-petaled lotus flower; within that lotus, place a vajra in the eastern position, a jewel in the southern position, a lotus in the western position, and a sword in the northern position.
Having thus constructed the maṇḍala, the ācārya shall bathe himself, purify himself through fasting and observance, and adorn his body with various ornaments.

At that time, he shall fill an arghya-vase with scented water, insert various flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves, and cover the arghya-vase with a fresh, clean cloth. The ācārya, according to the ritual, empowers the vase, filling it with the perfumed water containing the five jewels, the five medicines, and the five grains.

The first arghya-vase is named the Most Victorious Vase (*paramavijaya-kalaśa*); it is the deity itself. There are four other vases, which represent the four attendant bodhisattvas and the gate-protectors; each of the vidyārājas likewise has an arghya-vase.
If one does not intend to place the vases according to the various ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*), one should simply set out five vases.

One should empower the *argha* vases with the *sarvasiddhi-mantra* and sprinkle the *argha* water upon all sentient beings to purify them; thereafter, one should present incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, and various kinds of food and drink as offerings of emanation.
Furthermore, one should place a single *argha* vase at each of the four corners of the maṇḍala, and install the first and most excellent vase in the center of the maṇḍala.
At that time, the ācārya, using the fundamental mudrā of the Vajra Hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*) and reciting the mantra, invites all the Tathāgatas to enter the maṇḍala.
At that time, the ācārya further visualizes the offering of seats, with all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas seated in their respective original positions within the maṇḍala.

Next, he visualizes outside the maṇḍala the establishment of a boundary by driving in vajra-pestles. He then makes offerings of arghya water, incense, flowers, and so forth, while binding each of the fundamental mudrās.
At that time, the ācārya praised all the noble sages, shook the vajra bell, and offered various kinds of music. Having paid his respects to the Buddhas and noble sages, he addressed them, saying:
"I now seek the methods for all accomplishments."
Having spoken thus, he causes the disciple to enter the maṇḍala.
At that time, the ācārya recites the secret mantras of the five Tathāgatas and places them upon the five locations of the disciple’s body.
The mantras are as follows:

“Oṃ jina-garbha,” “Oṃ vajra-tīkṣṇa,” “Oṃ ratna-tīkṣṇa,” “Oṃ aruṇa,” “Oṃ prajñā-tīkṣṇa. With these mantras, one should respectively form their respective root mudrās and place them upon the five locations of the disciple to serve as armor.
At that time, the Ācārya covers the disciple’s face with silk, leads him before the maṇḍala, and recites this gāthā:

“*Eka-dur-darśana-maṇḍala-svāraṃ | Vajrajñāna-syaprapanna | Praveśitu māya-śiṣya | Sarva-tathāgatān pūraya.*” Having recited this gāthā, he then instructs the disciple to form the Sattvavajra mudrā and cast a flower into the center of the maṇḍala, while reciting this mantra:
"Oṃ pratisaṃvara hu. Having recited this mantra, remove the cloth covering the face and recite this gāthā:
"Idaṃ tanmaṇḍalaṃ paśya śraddadhāna avināśa."
MUDRĀṂ SAṄKOCAYA SVĀHĀ | MĀRA-PARĀJAYE TIṢṬHA SAMYAK-SIDDHINAM || 3 ||
*Samayaṃkruvāviṣati vajrapadmagrahara liṃda maṃtrīśvara dhanakru aninahriṇaye nayāśa vajraprati.* Having recited this verse, have the disciple throw a flower;

wherever the flower falls, that shall be his tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Then, perform sublime offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, clothing, banners, pennants, parasols, mudrās, and powders, and further offer exquisite music and auspicious verses of praise.

At that time, the Ācārya first uses the most excellent *argha* flask to confer empowerment upon the disciple, thereby eliminating defilements; subsequently, having conferred empowerment with the four *argha* flasks of the close attendants (*upāsaka*), he further recites auspicious verses of praise and addresses the disciple, saying:
"I now vibrate the bell before all Buddhas, Whose forms pervade everywhere like mustard seeds.
All Buddhas uphold this *argha* flask, Bestowing upon you the sublime gateway of empowerment."
The true wisdom of the mind-maṇḍala—contemplate such signless dharmas as these;
now receive this dharma-gate upon the crown of your head, and forever transcend the realm of worldly toil and birth-and-death.

At that time, having recited this auspicious praise, the ācārya instructs the disciple in the ritual methods of the śalākā-wheel, the conch, and the vajra, as well as the use of substances such as gold and silver, all for the purpose of removing their obscurations and hindrances.
If items such as śalākā (lotus stalks) are not available, one should instead bind the *rubhini* mudrā and show it to the disciple, and then bestow the samaya dharma.
The samaya mantra is as follows: "Oṃ āḥ jñaiḥ prabṛtti-danavātsa."
Vidiṛdhastitviviśana sadharma ṛticidantañca ācarīya mava-maheṣṇa.
VAJRA-PATIR-ŚŪKĀRAMCA NAṢṬA-MĀTRE VIGATA PRANĀPATE VACA.
Nāgārjuna-maitreya-jñāna (8) iddhi-kṛti-nive-buddha (9) naraka-kṣīra-pota-ye-tite (10). At that time, having recited this samaya-mantra,

the ācārya exhorted the disciple to offer wealth and treasures as a repayment for the teacher’s kindness— whether gold, silver, lapis lazuli, maṇi-jewels, pearls, coral, amber, or even his own body and life— and further spoke these verses:
"A disciple should practice filial piety, repaying the kindness of the ācārya so as to bring him joy;
if the teacher is joyful, the Dharma will be accomplished—for beyond this, there is no one more venerable in the world."
At that time, having heard this verse, the disciple rose from his seat, made offerings to the Buddhas and the ācārya, and thereafter the ācārya performed the homa according to the ritual rules.

Regarding the materials for the homa offering and the visualization methods for recitation, one should make offerings to all Buddhas and worthy sages according to the rituals for pacification, enrichment, and so forth. Then, having dismissed the worthy sages and the Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should collect the five-colored powders from within that mandala and cast them into a river, and smear the site of the mandala with *gomaya* (cow dung).
All items used within the maṇḍala must be offered entirely to the ācārya; the disciple may not accept them, for should he accept them, he would violate the samaya.
Only the ācārya may use them as he pleases.

Chapter Three: The Mantra Chapter At that time, the Bhagavān, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, again entered the Vajra-samādhi called "The Turning of the Mantra Wheel. Emerging from this samādhi, he addressed the Great Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Listen now with close attention!
"I shall now expound for you these sublime and wondrous syllables of the mantra; receive and uphold them with a sincere mind.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Well-spoken, World-Honored One! Well-spoken, Sugata! It is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke:

Chapter Four: The Chapter on Samādhi At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, entered the samādhi called "The Perfect Manifestation of Great Wisdom-Power. Emerging from this concentration, he addressed the Great Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Listen attentively now!"

I shall now explain for you the secret samādhi-dharmas of all mantras, so that the vidyādhara may thoroughly understand the maṇḍala and, by visualizing the painted images of the Buddhas and other forms according to the ritual rules, attain ultimate great wisdom and realize unsurpassed bodhi without difficulty; how much more so regarding the dharmas of accomplishment sought.

Now, the method for *samādhi* is explained: from within one’s own body, one visualizes the syllable *Oṃ*, which transforms into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*). Using wisdom to open and draw forth this Great Wisdom, it transforms into the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana. His body is of true golden color and has three faces, all of which are perfected with auspicious marks. He wears a jeweled crown upon his topknot, and his body possesses six arms: the two primary hands form the *dhyāna-mudrā*; the second left hand holds the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the third holds a bow; the second right hand holds a wheel, and the third holds an arrow. His bodily radiance is intensely blazing, such that all devas and humans are struck with awe. Emanated Buddhas appear like clouds, which are then withdrawn back into the body of the Buddha Mahāvairocana.

At that time, the Ācārya contemplates the subtle syllables and visualizes the Absolute Truth. Furthermore, the method of *samādhi* is explained: again, one visualizes the syllable *Aḥ* within the mouth.

This syllable *Aḥ* transforms into Amitāyus Buddha, whose body is white in color, with six arms and three faces, each face having three eyes. He wears a jeweled crown upon his head, and within the crown resides the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa amidst a topknot of flowing hair. Adorned with every ornament, his two [primary] hands open lotus flowers; his right second hand holds a vajra, and his third hand holds a rosary; his left second hand holds the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, and his third hand grasps a water flask (*kuṇḍikā*). His radiance is blazing and illuminates his entire body. He manifests transformations of vajras, causing all māras to be struck with terror, to fall into confusion, and to collapse to the ground.
In this way, the ācārya who visualizes the Vajra of Speech will realize awakening before long.
This is called the Samādhi of the Supreme and Extensive Dharma-Treasury of All Aspects.

Furthermore, the method for *samādhi* is explained: At that time, the *ācārya* visualizes his own fundamental mind as a lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*). This lunar disc transforms into the syllable *HŪṂ*. The syllable *HŪṂ* transforms into Akṣobhya Buddha, whose body is the color of emerald, possessing eight arms and three faces, each face having three eyes. He wears a jeweled crown, and his physical form is exquisitely beautiful and adorned with all ornaments. His first right hand holds a vajra; the second holds a sharp sword; the third holds a hook (*aṅkuśa*); and the fourth holds an arrow. His first left hand holds a bell (*ghaṇṭā*); the second holds the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; the third holds a noose (*pāśa*); and the fourth holds a bow.
One should thus visualize the Buddha Akṣobhya as pervading all of space.
At that time, if the ācārya constantly contemplates with a mind fixed in the vajra-samādhi, he will before long realize great bodhi.

This is called the *Vajra Infinite Samādhi of the Great Mind Perfected by Transcending Old Age and Death*. Furthermore, the method for this samādhi is explained: At that time, the ācārya visualizes the syllable *Traṃ* transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

This Great Wisdom transforms into the Buddha Ratnasaṃbhava, whose body is red in color, with four arms and three faces, each face having three eyes. His auspicious marks are perfectly complete; he wears a jeweled crown upon his head and is adorned with various precious ornaments. He sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), with his two primary hands forming the mudrā of meditative concentration (*dhyānamudrā*). His second right hand holds a vajra, and his second left hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). Filling the entirety of space, he manifests as Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava, raining down great jewels and emanating various bodhisattvas.
This is called the *Ratnasambhava-mahājñānavajra-samādhi*. Furthermore, the method for this samādhi is explained:

At that time, the ācārya visualizes the syllable *Khaṃ* transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*). This Great Wisdom transforms into the Buddha Amoghasiddhi, whose body is green in color and has four arms. His two primary hands form the *dhyāna-mudrā*; his second right hand holds a sharp sword, and his second left hand holds a hook. He emanates all Buddhas like rain filling the sky, performing all rites of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and emitting great radiance no different from the ocean of wisdom.
Visualizing the Great Muni Ākāśagarbha in this manner, that person becomes equal to space, free from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
This is called the "Great Wisdom Vajra Samādhi of the Nature of Space."
Having thus explained the *samādhi* rites of the five Tathāgatas, he further explained the visualization method for the four attendant Bodhisattvas.

At that time, the *ācārya* visualized [the deity] as having a radiant color and all manner of ornaments, with eight arms and three faces, each face possessing three eyes, and endowed with perfect auspicious marks. His first right hand forms the *varada-mudrā*, the second forms the *abhaya-mudrā*, the third holds a *vajra*, and the fourth holds an arrow. His first left hand holds a noose, with the index finger extended upward to form the *pratijñā-mudrā*; the second holds a branch of a jewel tree, the third holds a rosary, and the fourth holds a bow. He emits red light, from which emanated transformation Buddhas like clouds.
Visualizing the Great Wisdom Vajra in this manner, all the devas are struck with awe and fear, and they all join their palms in prostration.
Visualizing the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā thus, adorned with the power of the factors of enlightenment—this is called the Samādhi of the Great Wisdom Vajra Transformation of Buddhalocanā.
Furthermore, the method for *samādhi* is explained: At that time, the *ācārya* visualizes the syllable *MĀṂ* transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

This Great Wisdom transforms into the Bodhisattva Māmakī, whose body is the color of an *utpala* flower. She has six arms and three faces, each face having three eyes that emit red light. Her first right hand forms the *abhaya-mudrā*, the second holds a vajra, and the third holds an arrow. Her first left hand forms the *tarjanī-mudrā*, the second holds a noose (*pāśa*), and the third holds a bow. She emanates all Buddhas like rain filling the sky.
Thus, one should visualize the Great Power Vajra of the Three Bodies, manifesting with signs from the signless; this is called the profound samādhi of the great wisdom-power born of illusion.
"Furthermore, the method for *samādhi* is explained. At that time, the *ācārya* visualizes the syllable *baṃ* transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

This Great Wisdom transforms into the Bodhisattva Pāṇḍaravāsī, whose body is white in color, possessing six arms and three faces, each face having three eyes, and adorned with all ornaments. His first right hand forms the *abhaya-mudrā*, the second holds a vajra, and the third holds an arrow; his first left hand holds a lotus, the second holds a rosary, and the third holds a bow. Seated in the *paryaṅka* posture, he visualizes transformation Buddhas arising from the lotus, filling the entire realm of space like clouds."
By visualizing this samādhi in this manner, such a person shall attain supreme bodhi.
This is called the Lotus Supernatural Power, Supreme Buddha-Wisdom Vajra Samādhi.
Furthermore, the method for *samādhi* is explained: At that time, the *ācārya* visualizes the syllable 𑖮 (Dhaṃ) transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

This Great Wisdom transforms into the Bodhisattva Tārā, her various marks complete, her body green in color, with six arms and three faces, each face having three eyes. She sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), emitting red light that fills and blazes everywhere as a manifestation. Visualize all Buddhas filling the void, and the Bodhisattva as the mother of all sentient beings. Her first right hand forms the *abhaya-mudrā*, the second holds a vajra, and the third holds an arrow; her first left hand forms the *tarjanī-mudrā*, the second holds an *utpala* flower, and the third holds a bow.
This is called the Samādhi of the Vajra of Great Bliss Wisdom that Subjugates All Sentient Beings.
Furthermore, the method for this samādhi is explained:
at that time, the ācārya should visualize the four attendant bodhisattvas, namely, Sattvavajra Bodhisattva, Ratnavajra Bodhisattva, Dharmavajra Bodhisattva, and Karmavajra Bodhisattva.
Having performed the visualization as previously described, one will realize great enlightenment before long.
This is called the Samādhi of Rejoicing in the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, the method for this samādhi is explained:

At that time, the ācārya visualizes the syllable *BHRŪṂ* transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*), which further transforms into the Bodhisattva Cundā; she is then praised and extolled by the three bodies (*trikāya*) of seven koṭis of Tathāgatas.

The mantra of this Bodhisattva consists of nine syllables; it also constitutes the ninefold dharma and forms the nine Great Bodhisattvas. Their bodies are like the color of autumn moonlight, adorned with various jewels, and their marks are perfectly complete; they are able to deliver all worthies and sages.

This Bodhisattva has twenty-six arms and three faces, each face having three eyes. The central face is of auspicious appearance and smiles; the right face is a deep blue color and displays a wrathful expression, with sharp fangs like a crescent moon and a tongue like a flash of lightning; the left face is yellow and bites its lip.
This Bodhisattva, whether sitting or standing in a posture like a dancing performance, joins his two hands in the root mudrā placed at his heart;
his second right hand forms the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) mudrā; his third hand holds a sword;
his fourth hand holds a precious necklace (*ratnamālā*); his fifth hand holds a sea-sweet fruit (*sāgarasvādu-phala*); and his sixth hand holds an arrow.
The seventh hand holds a battle-axe; the eighth hand holds a jeweled staff; the ninth hand holds a bone-mallet;
the tenth hand holds a hook; the eleventh hand holds a vajra; the twelfth hand forms the mudrā of threat;
the thirteenth hand holds a rosary; and the second left hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel.
The banner; in the third hand he holds a lotus flower, in the fourth hand he holds a kamaṇḍalu,
in the fifth hand he holds a noose, in the sixth hand he holds a bow, in the seventh hand he holds a śakti, in the eighth hand he holds a wheel,
in the ninth hand he holds a conch shell, in the tenth hand he performs the *kṛtaka* mudrā, and in the eleventh...
Holding the *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious vase) in his [left] hand, he holds a *piṇīpala* (betel nut) in his twelfth hand and the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in his thirteenth hand.
Seated upon a lotus throne, his entire body radiates light.

He wears an *acchaka* robe, leaving one shoulder bare, with a net-like sash draped across his armpits, and is adorned with various garments and ornaments. Emanations of Buddhas fill the entirety of space.
Emptiness.

Thus, when the Bodhisattva Cunda possessed such great supernormal powers, all the devas, māras, and others were struck with awe and fear; they all came forward, joined their palms, and prostrated themselves in worship.

If an ācārya constantly contemplates and maintains this mantra in this manner, that person will before long realize great enlightenment (mahābodhi). If they enter this samādhi, they can eliminate all sins in a single instant; how much more so for other methods of accomplishment?
This is called the Supreme Samādhi of the Great Vajra of Boundless Victorious Wisdom-Tīrṇa of Great Power.
Furthermore, the method for this samādhi is explained: At that time, the ācārya visualizes the syllable *RĀṂ* transforming into Great Wisdom.

This Great Wisdom transforms into the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha, whose body is of true golden color and who sits in the full lotus posture. He has six arms and three faces, each face having three eyes; all his marks are perfect, his countenance is smiling, and he is adorned with various jewels. His two [primary] hands hold jewels from which light radiates. His second right hand forms the mudrā of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), and his third right hand holds an arrow. His second left hand forms the mudrā for threatening all evils, and his third left hand holds a bow. His body emits red light, and emanated Buddhas fill the void like clouds.
Visualizing this Bodhisattva, the supreme treasury of the wondrous Dharma, one can eliminate all evils and attain enlightenment before long.
This is called the Samādhi of the Illumination of Buddha-Wisdom from the Jewel Cloud.
Furthermore, the method for *samādhi* is explained: At that time, the *ācārya* visualizes the syllable *BHRŪṂ* transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

This Great Wisdom transforms into the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī, who is able to deliver beings from all fears. Her body is the color of autumn moonlight; she has six arms and three faces, each with three eyes, manifesting expressions of both wrath and joy. Her radiance is blazing and intense. In her first right hand she holds a vajra, in the second a jeweled staff, and in the third an arrow. In her first left hand she holds a noose while forming the *kṣepaka-mudrā*, in the second she holds a water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*), and in the third a bow. Emanated Buddhas appear like clouds.
Thus, by constantly performing this visualization while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one can eliminate all fears and will certainly attain Bodhi.
This is called the Great Wisdom Vajra Samādhi that Eliminates All Fears.
Furthermore, the method for *samādhi* is taught: At that time, the *ācārya* visualizes the syllable HŪṂ transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

This Great Wisdom transforms into the Bodhisattva Vajraśṛṅkhalā, the Mother of all Buddhas who can subdue malevolent sentient beings. Her body is green in color, with six arms and three faces; each face has three eyes and displays a smiling expression. She is adorned with various jewels. In her first right hand she holds a vajra, in her second a vajra-chain, and in her third an arrow. In her first left hand she forms the *kīlana-mudrā*, in her second she holds a noose, and in her third a bow. Emanated Buddhas appear like clouds.
By visualizing the Bodhisattva Vajraśṛṅkhalā in this manner, that person will realize great awakening before long, let alone other methods of accomplishment.
This is called the Vajrasamādhi of Great Wisdom for Liberation through the Vajra Chain.
Furthermore, the method for *samādhi* is explained: At that time, the *ācārya* visualizes the syllable 𑖮 (mai) transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

This Great Wisdom transforms into the Bodhisattva Maitreya, who has four arms and three faces, each face having three eyes. He sits in the full lotus posture upon a lotus flower; his two primary hands form the *dharmacakra-mudrā*, and his second right hand forms the *varada-mudrā*. For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, his second left hand holds a nāga-flower staff. He emanates various Buddhas and transformed Bodhisattvas that fill the sky like clouds.
Visualizing in this manner, the merit obtained is no different from that previously described.
This is called the "Samādhi of Maitreya’s Great Power and Supreme Wisdom.
Furthermore, the method for this samādhi is explained:

At that time, the Ācārya visualizes the syllable *Mum* transforming into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*). This Great Wisdom transforms into the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, appearing in the form of a youth, endowed with great eloquence and supreme wisdom, skillfully preaching the sublime Dharma. He has three faces, each with three eyes, and three topknots upon his head, with Akṣobhya Buddha crowning them. He sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) upon a lotus flower, his body adorned with various flowers. His physical marks are perfectly complete and he wears a gentle smile. He possesses six arms: the first right hand forms the *varada-mudrā* (gesture of granting boons), the second holds a sword, and the third holds an arrow; the first left hand holds the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the second holds an *utpala* flower, and the third holds a bow. Emanated Buddhas appear like clouds.
Visualizing in this manner yields great benefits no different from those previously mentioned.
This is called the "Samādhi of the Wondrous Vajra of Great Wisdom Light.
At that time, having taught this method of samādhi, the World-Honored One further spoke on the methods of visualization for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas:
“Namely: the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin, the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla,
the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānakuṭa, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
the Bodhisattva Sarvapāpāvaraṇaviśodhana, the Bodhisattva Sarvadaurmanasyāndhakāravidhamana, and the Bodhisattva Jvalanaprabha...”
The Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, the Bodhisattva Amṛtaprabha, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, and other such countless asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—
if all sentient beings visualize each of them according to the aforementioned ritual procedure, these subtle and wondrous syllables will transform into great wisdom.
The Bodhisattvas of Great Wisdom and Transformation each have three faces, with three eyes on each face;
they may have four or six arms, each holding their respective insignia and manifesting supernatural transformations.

If a person maintains sincere resolve and recites [the mantra] continuously according to the ritual, that person will before long swiftly attain accomplishment in the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood, benefiting all beings.
"May all sentient beings be happy.

At that time, the ācārya visualizes the HŪṂ-KING, with a solar disc as his halo, blazing intensely.
Like the fire at the end of an eon, his body is the color of a dark blue cloud; he is short in stature with a large belly, possessing six arms, six feet, and six faces, each face having three eyes.
His primary face has its mouth agape in a great wrathful expression, with sharp vajra fangs protruding outward and a tongue like a flash of lightning.
He bears the Buddha Akṣobhya upon his crown, and from his right face, his tongue extends outward.
The left face bites its lip in a wrathful expression and bears the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī upon its crown;
the first right hand holds a sharp sword, the second holds a vajra, and the third holds an arrow;
the first left hand holds a noose while forming the *kṛkāṭaka* mudrā, and the second holds the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
In his third hand he holds a bow; he wears a garment of tiger skin adorned with eight dragons, and a crown of skulls.
His hair-tuft is yellow, and he rides upon a water buffalo.
He is seated upon a lotus throne and extends his right leg downward, causing all the māras below to tremble with fear; he is also named "The Subduer of Yama."

O King, possessing great eloquence, with a radiance of crimson hue and emanating clouds of transformation Buddhas—such an Ācārya remains constantly in this contemplation throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Even if he were to experience the pleasures of the five desires, his mind would be like space, entirely free from attachment; the merit he thereby acquires will be immeasurable and boundless.
This is called the Samādhi of the Great Wisdom Vajra that Accomplishes All Deeds, which Subdues the Lord of the Flame-Māras and Tames All Māras.
Furthermore, the method for this samādhi is explained:

This Great Wisdom transforms into the wrathful Vidyārāja Prajñāntaka, who has six arms and three faces, each face having three eyes. His central face smiles, and he bears Akṣobhya Buddha upon his crown. His right face is blue and manifests a wrathful expression; his left face is white and bites its lip with its teeth. In his first right hand he holds a vajra, in the second a jeweled staff, and in the third an arrow. In his first left hand he holds a noose while forming the *kīlana-mudrā*, in the second he holds the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and in the third a bow.
Having thus visualized the transformations of supernatural powers and constantly reciting [the mantra], this person will before long realize great bodhi.
This is called the "Invincible Great Wisdom Vajra Samādhi."

at that time, the ācārya visualizes the syllable *MĀṂ* transforming into Great Wisdom, and that Great Wisdom transforms into the sun.

at that time, the ācārya visualizes the syllable *baṃ* transforming into great wisdom, and that great wisdom transforms into an alms-bowl.

Adorned with all ornaments, his right hands hold a vajra in the first, an axe in the second, and an arrow in the third;

The Manifestation of the Great Wisdom of Mantras. At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, having surveyed all the Tathāgatas, entered the samādhi of the Supreme Vajra of Quiescence and Freedom from Dust. Emerging from this samādhi, he spoke from the Vajra-samaya the mantra of the Great Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā, the Mother of All Tathāgatas, as follows: [Mantra follows]

"Oṃ vagavati ruru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddharuñjani sarvārthasādhani svāhā. At that time, when all the Tathāgatas and the assembly of Great Bodhisattvas who have perfected the ten stages heard this mantra, they were all filled with joy; all the demonic armies became terrified and bewildered, thinking only of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra.

"This mantra is now fully endowed with great wisdom; if there are those who uphold and recite it, they can accomplish various feats of siddhi, even restoring life to the dead, and achieving that which is difficult to achieve."

At that time, the World-Honored One again entered the Vajra-Samādhi of the Most Supreme Blazing Triple-Vajra. Emerging from this meditative absorption, he spoke the mantra of the Mother of All Buddhas, Bodhisattva Māmakī, saying:

“Oṃ śaṅkari śāntikari kṛta kṛta kṛtti kṛtti ṛgataya ṛgataya kṛtti svāhā. Thereupon, having heard this mantra of the Mother of Buddhas, all the Tathāgatas were filled with great joy and focused their minds solely upon the Tathāgata Citta-Vajra.
"This mantra can accomplish all rites for pacifying calamities, increasing prosperity, and so forth; it can provide protection, and even extinguish all karmic obstacles and hindrances."

At that time, the World-Honored One again entered the *vajra-samādhi* of the transformation of the heart of the three *vajras* within the Great Bliss Infinite Lotus, and having emerged from that concentration, he spoke from the three *vajras* the mantra of the Mother of All Dharmas, the White-Robed Bodhisattva (*Pāṇḍaravāsini*), as follows:
“Oṃ kaṭe vikaṭe ni-kaṭe kaṇkaṭe karuṇā-mayī svāhā. At that time, having heard this mantra, all the Tathāgatas emerged from their concentrations and dwelt solely upon the mind-*vajra* Tathāgata.
"If a person maintains this recitation and visualization, they will be able to accomplish all tasks, provide excellent protection, and even increase the subtle treasury of the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One again entered the Samādhi of the Great Bliss Vajra of the Equality of the Three Vajras that Awakens All Devas; having emerged from meditative absorption, he spoke the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñātārā, the Mother of All Buddhas, as follows:
"Oṃ tāri tātāri ture svāhā. At that time, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, upon hearing this mantra, were filled with great joy and contemplated only the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra.

At sunrise, sitting facing the sun, they should first visualize the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra; next, visualize the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī; and next, visualize the Great Vidyārāja Yamāntaka, holding a vajra-hook, his entire body radiant with light, manifesting a great wrathful form. Having done so, one should then recite the mantra of the Vidyārāja to empower the vermilion and other substances, and write down the name of the person to be summoned—including even nāga maidens, yakṣa maidens, as well as Nārāyaṇa and Maheśvara—whereupon they will all be struck with terror and quickly appear before one.

If one does not perform the visualization according to the ritual, the dhāraṇī for summoning will ultimately fail to achieve its result; however, if one recites it in accordance with these instructions, whatever one desires shall certainly be accomplished.
And he spoke in verse:
"The Great Bodhisattva Vajrasattva, Who is well able to perfect the vajra-mind;
If one recites according to the ritual in continuous succession, All undertakings shall be accomplished."

At that time, the World-Honored One again entered the Great Wisdom Transformation Vajra Samādhi. Emerging from this meditative absorption, he spoke the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahā-krodha-vajra from the Three Vajras, saying:

"Oṃ śūlini svāhā. At that moment, upon hearing this mantra, all the nāga maidens were struck with terror; their bodies seemed to blaze like fire, and they could think of nothing but the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra.
"If one contemplates and recites this mantra of the Great Bodhisattva according to the ritual, it can hook all nāgas and nāga maidens; adorned and beautiful, they will all appear before one."

At that time, the World-Honored One again entered the samādhi of the "Transformational Superknowledge of the Great Ocean Equal to Space"; having emerged from this concentration, he spoke the mantra of the Great Venerable Bodhisattva from the Three Vajras, saying:

“Namaḥ samyaksaṃbuddhagocare | Tadyathā | Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe svāhā. At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this mantra of the Bodhisattva Cundā, all the Buddha-fields shook violently; all the great Bodhisattvas emerged from their *samādhi*, and all the hosts of Māras, as well as the yakṣas and the daughters of the asuras, were struck with fear and terror, suffering great agony as if their bodies were being consumed by fire, and they could think of nothing but the Great All-Illuminating Vajra Tathāgata.
“If any person should visualize according to this rite and recite this Bodhisattva’s mantra with a sincere mind, all that they seek shall be fully accomplished.

At that time, the World-Honored One again entered the Samādhi of the Supreme Vajra of Ākāśagarbha; having emerged from this concentration, he spoke from the Three Vajras the Great Dharma Nectar Mantra of Bhṛkuṭī Bodhisattva, saying:

“Oṃ vayanāśani trāsani trāsaya trāsaya bṛkuṭi taṭi veṭāli śveti śvetajarati svāhā. At that time, when all the Vidyādharīs and the various devas heard this mantra of the Great Bodhisattva, they were all struck with terror, their bodies and minds trembling; all the māras fled in fear, thinking only of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra.

"If this mantra is recited according to the ritual rules, it can also summon great powerful nāgas and nāga maidens, asuras and asura maidens, yakṣas and yakṣa maidens, and so forth, causing them all to appear before one."
If one recites it ten million times (*koṭi*), one can subdue all māras and effectively accomplish all rites of siddhi.

Furthermore, if there is anyone who slanders the ācārya, slanders the Mahāyāna sūtras, or even the secret mantras, yet nonetheless performs the recitation of this most supreme dharma, that person shall be beset by obstacles created by evil māras; the rite will not be accomplished and will instead be self-destructive.

If a person reveres the teacher and the Dharma as they would the Buddha, and practices for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings through meditative visualization, then everything this person does and seeks will be accomplished, and they shall further realize great enlightenment before long.
Furthermore, the method for accomplishment is explained:

If a practitioner of recitation wishes to perform a rite of subjugation, they should use a garment dyed with *rudhira* (blood). Having put on this garment, they should visualize their own body as the Vidyārāja, manifesting a wrathful aspect and treading upon the form of the māra with both feet. While reciting the mantra of the Vidyārāja, that māra will be naturally eliminated before long.

Alternatively, using *śāli* cloth to dye one's robes, one should visualize the Vidyārāja as before, manifesting in a wrathful form and treading upon Māra with his feet; by reciting the mantra, that Māra will likewise be spontaneously eliminated.

Alternatively, using a dyed cloth of *mumtra*, visualize it according to the previous ritual method; by reciting the mantra while treading upon the effigy of the māra, one shall likewise cause its destruction.

Alternatively, using robes dyed with *batsamana*, one should assume the form of a great wrathful deity as before and recite the mantra one thousand times; all those māras and obstructors will then be completely extinguished.

If the practitioner who maintains the recitation thoroughly understands the ritual procedures for the mudrās and, according to the preceding instructions, performs the visualization and recitation in accordance with the Dharma, they will be able to subjugate all sentient beings within the three realms.
"Furthermore, the locations for recitation shall be explained:

namely, the abodes of the seven mothers, or within a śmaśāna forest, or inside an empty house, or in a place where a celestial deity dwells alone, or beneath a great tree, or at a crossroads. Having selected such a site, one should perform the rite of subjugation (*abhicāra*). First, the reciter takes a human bone eight finger-widths long to serve as a ritual stake (*kīla*). Taking earth from beneath the feet of the person to be subdued, he fashions an image of that person. After empowering the stake by reciting the root mantra eight hundred times, he drives it into the image."

Thereafter, take this image and secretly bury it within the ground outside the door of that person's house; within half a month, they will swiftly come to submit, or if they do not submit, they will quickly be destroyed of their own accord—this cannot be undone.
"Furthermore, regarding the method for accomplishment:

the practitioner first takes a skull that is undamaged and complete, and inscribes the mantra within it. Having empowered it according to the ritual, one may secretly bury it outside the gate of the person to be subdued, as previously described, or do so within a village; this will swiftly cause that person to be subdued and dispatched."
"Furthermore, regarding the method for accomplishment:

the reciter should write the mantra upon *bīḍa* leaves, birch bark, or silk cloth according to the ritual procedures as previously described, and secretly bury it outside the gate of that person's house; thus, subjugation will be swiftly attained."

At that time, after the World-Honored One, the Great Vairocana Vajra Tathāgata, had spoken this method of subjugation, he again entered the Great Wisdom Vajra Samādhi of the Three Vajra Kilas of all Tathāgatas. Emerging from this meditative absorption, from his body, speech, and mind—the three vajras—he spoke the mantra of the Great Wisdom Kila of the entire triple world, saying:
"Oṃ kha kha khādaya khādaya."

*Ka-ya va-kuñcita vajra-kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ.* At that time, having heard this mantra,
all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and focused their minds solely upon the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra.

"This mantra can eliminate all māras. When a practitioner of recitation wishes to perform this rite, they should fashion stakes from human bone, or from khadira wood, or from iron and the like. Once the stakes are prepared, one should employ the appropriate mudrās—namely, the fundamental mudrā of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, or the mudrā of Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha, or the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka, or the mudrās of the Vidyārājas Takkirāja and Mahābala—and subsequently visualize the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva with light radiating from his entire body; thus one performs the rite for subduing māras."

The practitioner, following the ritual of the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva, visualizes the body of that māra from crown to feet as being entirely staked with vajra-pestles, until the entire realm of space is filled with vajra-pestles. Thus, by practicing visualization and recitation according to the dharma while bringing the three karmas into correspondence, this Great Bodhisattva Vajrasattva is able to stake all māras.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana Vajra, again entered the samādhi of the Body-Wisdom Transformation Vajra; having emerged from this concentration, he spoke from his body, speech, and mind the non-dual mantra of the Body-Vajra Samaya, saying:

“Oṃ cina cini hana hana daha daha nighātaya vajrakīla hūṃ phaṭ. At that time, the *ācārya* forms the Vajra-mudrā and visualizes the Buddha Samantaprabha. He further visualizes this mantra as a vajra-kila and performs the gesture of driving in a kila. During the performance of this rite, even all the Buddhas emerge from meditative absorption and exclaim, “How marvelous! All hosts of Māras are completely subdued; if one does not act according to this, they shall be immediately destroyed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Vairocana-Vajra, again entered the *vajra-samādhi* of the Great Mind, Great Wisdom, and Vajra Transformation. Having emerged from this meditative absorption, he spoke from his three vajras—body, speech, and mind—the mantra of the Great Wrathful Kīla:

"Oṃ vajrarāja hūṃ. Then, after the ācārya has recited this mantra, he should visualize a five-pronged vajra filling the entirety of space. By the power of this mantra, he subdues all māras. Furthermore, visualizing the posture of driving in a kīla, he drives it into the midst of all the hosts of māras, whereby they are all completely subdued. If one does not rely on this method, one's body shall immediately perish.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, again entered the Samādhi of the Transformation Vajra of the Immeasurable Life Speech (*Amitāyus-vāk-samaya-vikurvita-vajra-samādhi*). Having emerged from this meditative absorption, he spoke this Kilaya-mantra from the samādhi of body, speech, and mind:

“Oṃ hrīḥ oṃ bhūḥ phaṭ. Then, the Ācārya, having recited this mantra, visualizes the Lotus Seal (*padma-mudrā*) blazing with intense radiance. Using the seal and form of the mantra, he subdues the māras and enemies, visualizing them as being pinned down by the force of a stake. If one recites and maintains this according to the ritual procedure, all hosts of māras will be completely subdued; if one does not follow the ritual procedure, they will certainly be eliminated.
"This true vajra-kila can nail down even if the entirety of space were filled with all manner of māras and enemies.

At that time, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana Vajra spoke this secret method of visualization for nailing the kila; that Tathāgata, his heart greatly rejoicing in the welfare of sentient beings, spoke these verses:
"The secret, wondrous Dharma, the primary meaning, Comprehensively encompassing the profound, true principle."
The supreme, inconceivable, and quiescent phrase Is the vajra stake of great wisdom.
It is the mantra that firmly nails down all malevolent spirits and demons, Even those who do not obey the Buddha’s commands.
This method of nailing with the stakes of all Buddhas Arises entirely from true and wondrous wisdom.
At that time, after the Bhagavān Mahāvairocana Vajra Tathāgata had spoken these verses, he again entered the *samādhi* of the Vajra of All Subtle Syllables.

Emerging from this meditative absorption, he spoke the mantra of the Bodhisattva Sūrya: "Oṃ marīciye devatāyai svāhā. At that time, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having heard this mantra, were filled with joy.

"This mantra-dharma can accomplish all tasks and eliminate the perils of enemies and bandits; if a person receives and maintains it according to the ritual, no evil whatsoever shall find an opportunity to harm them while traveling on the road."

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana Vajra, again entered the Samādhi of the Supreme Vajra of Great Wisdom Power for Subduing All Evil Māras and Skillfully Delivering All Sentient Beings. Having emerged from this concentration, he spoke the mantra of the Bodhisattva for Subduing the Trichiliocosm:

"Oṃ mahāsahasrapramardanī vara-siddhanaye maṇivajri hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. At that time, when the Bhagavān had spoken this mantra, all Buddha-fields shook violently; all Bodhisattvas emerged from their meditative absorptions (dhyāna); and all Māras were struck with terror, suffering great anguish as if their bodies were ablaze with fire.
They addressed the Buddha, saying: "We Māras, by virtue of the great power of this mantra, all suffer this anguish."
From this day forward, wherever this mantra may be held and recited, I vow not to create obstacles for them, but shall provide constant protection and cause their lifespan to increase.
At that time, the World-Honored One again entered the most supreme *samādhi* called "Saving Śakra and Subduing the Greatly Powerful Asuras.
Having emerged from this meditative absorption, he spoke the Supreme Jewel-Banner Dhāraṇī, saying: "Oṃ bhagavati tvajragri kevali..."

Together, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

"By the power of this Great Illumination, we hosts of Māras have experienced great suffering and affliction as if our bodies were ablaze with fire. From this day forward, we shall receive the Buddha’s samādhi and vow to perform all manner of supreme and wholesome deeds."

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana Vajra, again entered the samādhi of the Vajra Transformation of the Peaceful Matrix of All Beings; having emerged from this concentration, he spoke the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahāpratisarā:

"Oṃ maṇidhare vajriṇi mahāpratisare svāhā. At that time, when the Blessed One had spoken this mantra, all the great evil māras, enemies, and powerful spirits and deities—who constantly afflict sentient beings among humans and devour their fetuses—heard this great vidyā-mantra. They were all struck with terror as if fire were burning their bodies; they went before the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him, saying:
"Blessed One!"

"We, the various māras, having received the Buddha’s samādhi, shall from this day forward neither harm sentient beings nor consume fetuses; we shall protect all beings and bring them peace and security."

At that time, the Bhagavān Mahāvairocana Vajra Tathāgata again entered the samādhi of the Great Wisdom Vajra of Lokadhara. Emerging from this concentration, he spoke the mantra of the Bodhisattva Lokadhara:

“Oṃ vāsudhare mahāvāsudhare mṛtyunivartini vāsasvāhā. When the Bhagavān had spoken this mantra, all the hosts of Māras were utterly terrified; they thought only of the Bhagavān Mahāvairocana Vajra Tathāgata and addressed him, saying: “Bhagavān!”

If there are people who, regarding this mantra of the Bodhisattva Lokadhara, uphold, recite, copy, make offerings to, or invoke the name of this Bodhisattva, we, the hosts of Māras, shall rain down various precious treasures for those sentient beings to cause them to attain wealth and nobility.
At that time, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, again entered the *samādhi* called "Vajra of All Skillful Means for Subduing.
Emerging from this meditative absorption, he spoke the heart-mantra of the Rākṣasī Vidyujjvālāprabhā: "Oṃ hrūṃ dani prakoṣṭha-cāṇi."

At that time, when the Blessed One had spoken this heart-mantra of the Great Flashing Radiant Rākṣasī, all the great māra-enemies were utterly terrified; they experienced great suffering and torment as if their bodies were ablaze with fire.

"At that time, when a Vidyādhara wishes to perform this rite, he should first use a shroud. Having drawn the image of a Rākṣasī upon the shroud with blood or red earth, he should burn agallochum incense and perform an offering of birth with red flowers and red food. Then, having recited the heart-mantra eight hundred times, he should secretly bury this painted image in a śītavana (cemetery) while uttering the name of his enemy. While the image is thus buried, all māras and enemies will be completely bound and subdued, and the rites for producing *chi-mei* (goblins/phantoms) will be accomplished."
At that time, the Bhagavān Mahāvairocana Vajra Tathāgata again entered the *vajrasamādhi* known as "The Accomplishment of the Host of Hariti Yakṣiṇī Who Delights in Good Deeds.

Emerging from this meditative absorption, he spoke the mantra of the yakṣiṇī Haritī: "Oṃ harite mahāyakṣiṇi ye | hara hara | sarvabālān | sarvayakṣiṇī | praveśani svāhā ||" Then, having spoken this mantra of the great yakṣiṇī Haritī, the Bhagavān addressed the assembly:
"This mantra enables all yakṣiṇīs and their like to bring about every accomplishment for the practitioner who maintains its recitation."

At that time, while the practitioner performs this rite, they should visualize the eight-spoked wheel of the Wrathful Vidyārāja; within the wheel is the yakṣiṇī Hārītī, and upon the eight spokes of the wheel are the eight great yakṣiṇīs.
Having visualized this, one should further visualize oneself summoning these yakṣiṇīs and others with a hook, so that they all appear before one to perform the rites of accomplishment.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Vairocana-Vajra, again entered the samādhi called the Supreme Wisdom Vajra for Eliminating All Illnesses; having emerged from this concentration, he spoke the mantra of the Bodhisattva Parṇaśavarī:

“Oṃ piśācī pralaṃśavari sarvamārī-praśamani hūṃ phaṭ. At that time, when the Bhagavān had spoken this mantra, all the Buddha-fields shook violently; all the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and those capable of acting as Māras were utterly terrified, fell into confusion, and collapsed to the ground.

"At that time, when the practitioner wishes to perform the rite for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*), they should use *śara* grass, sesame seeds, milk, and branches from auspicious flowering or fruiting trees twelve finger-widths long as fuel. Following the ritual for *śāntika* homa, they should perform the homa while visualizing this Bodhisattva pervading the void and raining down nectar, whereby all demonic disturbances are entirely extinguished."
