Chapter Six: The Ritual for the Great Offering of Mudrās. At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana Vajra, addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Listen attentively now; I shall explain for you the Dharma of the Secret Mudrās born from the Great Wisdom of the Three Vajras."

If a practitioner of recitation forms mudrās according to the ritual, they can extinguish all karmic offenses; furthermore, by contemplating the ultimate truth, they will attain realization of unsurpassed bodhi—how much more so regarding other matters of accomplishment.
"Furthermore, regarding the method for forming the mudrās:
first, form fists with both hands and extend the two thumbs upright and level; this is the Body-Seal of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana."
Without altering the previous mudrā, place the left thumb inside the palm and extend the right thumb upright; this is the Samaya-mudrā of Amitāyus Buddha.
"Without altering the previous mudrā, insert the right thumb into the palm and extend the left thumb upright; this is the An-xin (Peace-of-Mind) mudrā of Akṣobhya Buddha."
"Again, form two fists with both hands; extend the index finger of the left hand vertically and insert it into the right fist. This is the fundamental mudrā of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana Vajra."

"Furthermore, sitting in the half-lotus posture with the left foot extended, placing the left hand at the navel wheel, and extending the right hand to touch the ground—this is the fundamental mudrā of Akṣobhya Buddha."
"Without altering the previous mudrā, form the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) with the right hand; this is the fundamental mudrā of Ratnasambhava Buddha.
Without altering the previous mudrā, place both hands at the navel in the gesture of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-mudrā*); this is the fundamental mudrā of Amitāyus Buddha."
“Without altering the previous mudrā, form the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) with the right hand; this is the fundamental mudrā of the Buddha Amoghasiddhi.
Furthermore, with both hands, form the vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*), and extend the two middle fingers upright like needles; this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Sattvavajra.”
“Without altering the previous mudrā, slightly bend the first joints of the two middle fingers so that they resemble the shape of a jewel; this is the mudrā of Ratnavajra Bodhisattva.
Without altering the previous mudrā, form a ring with the two middle fingers so that they resemble the shape of a lotus; this is the mudrā of Dharmavajra Bodhisattva.”
"Without altering the previous mudrā, form the two middle fingers like a *karmavajra*; this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Karmavajra.
Furthermore, join the two hands in *añjali*, and with the two index fingers, pinch the tips of the two thumbs in the shape of an eye; this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā."

"Furthermore, form the vajra-bind with both hands; extend the two middle fingers and join the tips of the two index fingers to the third joints of the middle fingers in the shape of a vajra. This is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Māmakī."
"Furthermore, join the two hands in *añjali* with the tips of the ten fingers not touching one another, slightly curved into the shape of a lotus; this is the mudrā of the lay bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, join the two hands in *añjali*; with the two index fingers, pinch the nails of the middle fingers, and place the two thumbs inside the palms so that they resemble the shape of an *utpala* flower. This is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Tārā."

"Furthermore, join the two hands in *añjali* (palms together); bend the two index fingers over the middle joints of the middle fingers like rings, and place the two thumbs at both sides. This is the mudrā of Bodhisattva Kuntī."
"Furthermore, with both hands forming the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*), slightly bend the first joints of the two index fingers and the two thumbs; this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhā."

"Furthermore, extend both hands; with the two thumbs, pinch the small fingernails, while the remaining fingers do not touch one another, forming the shape of a vajra. This is the mudrā of Bhṛkuṭī Bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, form two vajra-fists with both hands; interlace the little fingers and thumbs like a chain. This is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Vajrasaṃhāna."

"Furthermore, form two fists with both hands; let the two thumbs and little fingers be like needles, the two middle and ring fingers be turned away from each other, the two index fingers be bent toward the thumbs like rings, and the thumbs also be slightly bent like wheels. This is the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka."

"Furthermore, form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it at the heart; extend the index finger upright, while the right hand makes the gesture of grasping. This is the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Prajñāntaka."

"Furthermore, form two vajra-fists with both hands; interlace the two little fingers like a chain and place the two index fingers back-to-back like needles upon the forehead. This is the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Pañjaranātha."

"Furthermore, press the small fingernails with the thumbs of both hands, form the remaining fingers into the shape of a vajra, and cross the two hands to rest them upon the shoulders; this is the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Vajrānala."

"Furthermore, with the left hand, interlace the thumbs, ring fingers, and little fingers so that their nails are like the sheath of a sword; the right hand assumes the posture of grasping a sword. This is the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Acala."

"Furthermore, form two vajra-fists with the right hand placed above; the two fists are turned back-to-back, the two little fingers are interlaced like a lock, and the two index fingers are extended upward in the gesture of subjugation. This is the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Takkirāja."

"Furthermore, form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it at the heart; extend the index finger of the right hand and raise it upright like the shape of a staff. This is the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Nīlananda."
"Furthermore, place the left hand at the heart and form a fist with the right hand as if in the gesture of a swinging punch; this is the mudrā of Mahābalavajra.
Furthermore, form fists with both hands, and slightly extend the index fingers, thumbs, and middle fingers as if in the gesture of opening a flower; this is the mudrā of Maitreya Bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, join the two hands in *añjali*; with the index fingers, pinch the nails of the ring fingers in the manner of an *utpala* lotus. This is the mudrā of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, placing the left hand at the navel wheel and making the right hand into the 'elephant-posture' (hastivijṛmbhita), this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Gandhahasti.
Furthermore, forming a fist with the left hand held upright like a banner and making the right hand into the 'banner-posture' (patākā), this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu."
"Furthermore, sitting upon the seat of the virtuous, with both hands joined in *añjali* at the heart—this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.
Furthermore, extending both hands like the crawling motion of a tortoise with the fingers hooked within the palms—this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati."
"Furthermore, forming a vajra-fist with the left hand placed at the heart, while the right hand forms the mudrā of granting boons—this is the seal of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati."
"Furthermore, forming a fist with the left hand and placing it at the navel wheel while snapping the fingers with the right hand—this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Saṃbhadrakīrti.
Furthermore, forming both hands in the shape of a full-blown lotus—this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta."
"Furthermore, with both hands making the gesture of scattering [dust], this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Sarvapāpavināśana.
Furthermore, with both hands joined in *añjali* as if in the gesture of throwing, this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Sarvadaurmanasyāndhakāravidhvaṃsana."
"Furthermore, extending and stretching the fingers of both hands in the manner of blazing flames—this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Jvalanaprabha.
Furthermore, forming the gesture of granting boons (*varadamudrā*) with the right hand and holding the left hand in the shape of a lunar disc—this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Candraprabha."
"Furthermore, with both hands held like *argha* vases in the gesture of conferring empowerment, this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Amṛtaprabha.

Furthermore, with the left hand forming a vajra-fist placed at the navel, and the right hand also forming a fist in the gesture of rotating and stroking space, this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja."
"Furthermore, extend the left hand and place the index finger and thumb of the right hand within the palm of the left; this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin."

"Furthermore, form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it at the heart, extending the index finger; with the right hand, also form a vajra-fist and manifest a wrathful expression as if brandishing the fist. This is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Parṇaśavarī."

"Furthermore, with the left hand, place the thumb and index finger in the gesture of holding an object, and with the right hand, form the gesture of holding a needle; this is the Seal of the Bodhisattva of the Sun."

"Furthermore, forming the shape of a snake's head with both hands and placing them upon the crown of the head in the manner of a parasol, while slightly manifesting an expression of wrath—this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Śaṅkara, which can eliminate all poisons."
"Furthermore, as for the seal of the Vidyārāja Takkirāja mentioned previously: with the two index fingers held upright, this is the seal of the Vidyārāja Trailokyavijaya.

Without altering the previous seal, bend the right index finger like a hook to manifest a wrathful aspect; this is the Hook Seal (Ākarṣaṇamudrā) of the Vidyārāja Vajra. By employing this seal-method, one may summon all Tathāgatas."

"Furthermore, form two vajra-fists with both hands; bend the little fingers like fangs, interlace the two hands, and place them at the mouth. With fangs bared, tongue protruded, and a wrathful gaze, this is the mudrā of Vajradaṃṣṭravijaya."
Without releasing the previous mudrā, bend the two little fingers and the two index fingers into the shape of hooks; manifesting a wrathful gaze, this is the Vajra-Ḍākinī mudrā.
"Furthermore, form vajra-fists with both hands, extend both index fingers, and cross the two hands above the head, spreading them apart; this is the maṇḍala mudrā."
"Without altering the previous mudrā, after a long while, perform the *caṭasana* (scattering) hand gesture; this is the Gate-Opening Mudrā.

Furthermore, form fists with both hands, cross the two fists at the sides and clasp them there, manifesting an angry gaze and walking clockwise; this is the Mudrā for Destroying All Malevolent Planets."

"Furthermore, with the left hand extended and covered, place the right hand over the back of the left; moving the two thumbs—this is the mantra for destroying asuras and the mudrā for subduing asura women."

"Furthermore, interlace the thumbs and little fingers of both hands like a lock, with the remaining fingers held in the manner of banners; manifesting the appearance of great wrath, this is the mudrā of the Vajrapātāla Vidyārāja."
"Furthermore, with the left hand, form a vajra-fist and extend the index finger; this is the Vajrakīla mudrā.
Furthermore, with both hands, form a vajra-bind, and extend the two index fingers in the manner of driving in a kila-nail; this also is the Vajrakīla mudrā."
"Furthermore, form a vajra-fist with the right hand in the manner of striking with a mallet; this is the mallet seal (*mudrā*), which also constitutes the *ghaṇṭā* seal.
Furthermore, form vajra-fists with both hands, extend the two index fingers, and again assume the posture of the vajra-bind; this is the Vajrabandha seal of all Tathāgatas."
"Furthermore, form vajra-fists with both hands and then make the gesture of brandishing the fists; this is the Vajrakrodhaca mudrā."
"Furthermore, with both hands in the gesture of holding the moon, one strokes the face; then, extending them outward and displaying a wrathful gaze, this is the mudrā of the Rākṣasī Vidyutprabhā."
"Furthermore, interlace the two hands like a chain; extend the index fingers and thumbs upright in the manner of holding a sword. This is the Vajra Sword Mudrā; this mudrā can stop wind and rain."

"Furthermore, form fists with both hands, bend the two index fingers into rings, and manifest the appearance of great wrath; then extend both hands outward—this is the mudrā for destroying the mantras of others."

"Furthermore, covering the thumbs with both hands and tucking them inside the palms, moving the remaining fingers like wings, standing on one leg, extending the tongue, manifesting a wrathful gaze, and reciting the syllable *HŪṂ* continuously while walking according to the ritual procedure—this is the Garuḍa Mudrā. When this mudrā is bound, it can neutralize the poisons of the three realms."
"Furthermore, forming vajra-fists with both hands and then assuming the posture of shooting arrows in the four directions—this is the Vajra-Arrow Mudrā; this mudrā can destroy the armies of others."

"Furthermore, form two fists with both hands; let the two middle fingers be like needles, then bend them into the shape of jewels. Extend the two thumbs and press the tips of the nails of the index fingers together like rings. This is the Buddha’s Wheel Seal (Cakramudrā); this seal can rescue one from the perils of military conflict."
"Furthermore, form a fist with the left hand such that the middle finger is like a needle, and hold the right hand like a blossoming lotus; this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Halahala."

"Furthermore, form two fists with both hands, cross the two little fingers, and extend the two index fingers like needles; place them back-to-back upon the forehead. This is the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Hevajra; by means of this, one may enter the śmaśāna and destroy all malevolent spirits."
"Furthermore, with the left hand in the gesture of holding a skull and the right hand in the gesture of holding a trident, this is the mudrā of Maheśvara.

Furthermore, with the left hand extended so that the fingers do not touch one another in the gesture of fearlessness, the thumb tucked inside the palm, and the right hand made into a fist held upright in the gesture of holding a jeweled staff, this is the mudrā of Nārāyaṇa."
"Furthermore, with both hands extended and spread out in the shape of a lotus, this is the seal of Mahābrahmā.
Furthermore, with both hands joined in the *puṣpapuṭa* (flower) mudrā, this is the seal of the Mother of All Families."
"The mudrās formed by these four bodhisattvas who are close attendants—Sattvavajra and the others—should be identical to the initiation mudrās.
Once the ācārya has thus fully understood the methods for the mudrās of all the honored deities according to the maṇḍala, he must further fully understand the secret offerings within the maṇḍala."

"Having performed the gestures of offering with all the various performances of drama, garlands, song, and dance, as well as perfumes, flowers, lamps, and ointments—each according to the respective bodhisattva—and having likewise performed the gestures of offering for all such diverse ornaments, various exquisite garments, banners, pennants, parasols, and *argha* water, one should then ring the bell while holding the vajra and open the gate of the maṇḍala, reciting this mantra:"

“Oṃ vajrakhaṇḍarohā praraṇa sarapra-raṇa buddhacittācalini prajñāpāramitā nadasvabhāve vajradrahṛdaye santuṣyanti hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ. When the ācārya has recited this mantra, he shall cast the *vajra* with his right hand, ring the *vajra-ghaṇṭā* with his left hand, and immediately offer praise and worship to the noble deities with song.
"Having thus performed the supreme, true offering based upon the Vajra Mahāyāna, all Buddhas and noble sages are entirely delighted.
Those Tathāgatas then spoke these verses:
"If a person cuts off all doubts and delusions, And constantly practices the contemplation and visualization of Bodhi,"
Always with pure body, speech, and mind, making offerings to the noble ones is supreme.

If a person does not sever their various doubts, yet instead places faith and weight upon the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and practices the teachings of the Hīnayāna Śrāvaka, that person’s offering is not supreme.
"By making offerings to all Tathāgatas according to the Dharma, the sages and saints rejoice and exclaim that it is rare.
At that time, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, praised the Buddha Vairocana, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
He is able to analyze and reveal for sentient beings the Bodhi-dharma of the Great Yoga Teachings.
Then he spoke in verse:
“The Vajra of Pervasive Illumination and Perfect Wisdom, Expounds the gates of the Mahāyāna according to the capacities of beings.”
It can cause the severance of greed, hatred, and delusion, And allow one to contemplate the subtle and wondrous principle of Bodhi.
Excellent is the Unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma, Profound and vast, saving all sentient beings;
Such a true treasury of the Dharma-jewels Was proclaimed and expounded by that Buddha, the Great Awakened One.

At that time, having heard the subtle and wondrous sounds of the various Tathāgatas as they praised the Buddha in verse, all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy. They also praised the Buddha Samantaprabha in gāthās, saying:
“The Buddha’s body is boundless, without birth or extinction; It has no abiding, no speech, and no words.
It is quiescent, free from marks, like empty space; That which possesses marks is the Buddha’s skillful teaching.”
The teachings proclaimed bring merit to all living beings, Guiding them to ascend the stages of a bodhisattva;
That bodhisattvas may dwell within Buddha-fields Is entirely due to the secret samādhi.
At that time, after all the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas had each praised the Buddha with verses,
the Great Vairocana Vajra Tathāgata spoke this sublime song of praise:
"Vajra-hūṃ-jña-ye."

Chapter Seven: The Visualization of the Great Wisdom of Bodhicitta The Buddha-Spoken Yoga Mahātantrarāja Sūtra, Chapter Seven: The Visualization of the Great Wisdom of Bodhicitta. At that time, all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, with one voice, entreated the World-Honored One, the Great Vairocana-Vajra-Tathāgata:
“We pray that, out of compassion, you will expound the profound and unsurpassed Dharma of the Great Awakening of Bodhicitta.”
At that time, having accepted their request, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall now speak of it."
The Buddha said:

"This bodhicitta is itself the characteristic of the body; the nature of the body's characteristics being empty is true bodhi. Since the body has no distinction, the same applies to the characteristics of speech."

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s discourse, all the Tathāgatas dwelt within the three secrets of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas; with minds free from grasping and rejecting, they spoke these verses:
“Rare indeed is the body, speech, and mind of Samantabhadra, Primordially without arising or ceasing, and likewise without attachment.
Its essence is devoid of letters and all signs, Far removed from conceptual proliferation and transcending discrimination.”
At that time, after all the Buddhas had spoken these verses, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, entered the *vākcakravajra-samādhi*. Emerging from this meditative absorption, he declared:
"The bodhicitta is fundamentally free from arising and ceasing, for it is as profoundly tranquil and pure as space."
And he spoke in verse:
“The Bodhicitta is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; Its nature is pure, with no phenomena and nothing to be grasped.
Unattached and unstained like space— This is the firm and steadfast Bodhicitta.”

When Akṣobhya Tathāgata had spoken these verses, at that time Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata entered the *tathāgata-samādhi* of the formless vajra of all Tathāgatas. Emerging from this meditative absorption, he spoke of the bodhicitta, saying in verse:
“This nature is originally without nature; Its signless, unconditioned essence is solid and tranquil.”
"This Dharma originates from non-self; this is the adamantine bodhicitta.
Thus spoke the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava after reciting these verses.
At that time, the Tathāgata Amitāyus entered the samādhi of the Most Victorious and Blazing Vajra. Emerging from this meditative absorption, he spoke of the bodhicitta, declaring in verse:
“The realm of phenomena is fundamentally unarisen; It is tranquil, devoid of nature and devoid of marks.
Thoroughly penetrating the principle of emptiness without limit— This is the true mind of bodhi.”

After the Tathāgata Amitāyus had spoken these verses, the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi entered the samādhi of the Vajra of Unsurpassed Wisdom. Emerging from that meditative absorption, he spoke on the bodhicitta, saying in verse:
“The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure; Primordially quiescent and non-existent.”
There is neither awakening nor Buddha, Nor those sentient beings, nor the life-principle.
To see them as like a dream or a magical illusion— Even the vision of "no-seeing" is likewise so.
Free from existence and non-existence, with grasping and rejecting extinguished— This is the firm bodhicitta.
When the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi had spoken these verses,

at that time the Bodhisattva Maitreya and the other great Bodhisattvas, having heard how the Tathāgatas had taught the Dharma of the pure bodhicitta by means of the vajra body, speech, and mind, marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and spoke these verses:
“O Buddha, Most Supreme Honored One, You have excellently taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma.”
Dharmas arise from non-self; I prostrate to the bodhicitta.
Syllables arise from the letterless; the Buddha is manifested from the signless.
All things are like illusions and dreams; I prostrate to the vajra-mind.

After Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others had spoken these verses, the Great Vairocana Vajra Tathāgata further taught the visualization method: "The practitioner first sits in the full lotus posture and visualizes the five destinies, as well as what is appropriate and inappropriate.

By means of the mantra for purifying the three karmas, he thoroughly cleanses them all and establishes himself in the pure dharma. Thereafter, he visualizes his own fundamental mind as the syllable HŪṂ; the syllable HŪṂ transforms into the Buddha-body, and the Buddha-body is none other than one's own body. Manifesting a majestic and haughty bearing, he invites the worthy sages with the Vajra Hook. Having done so, he manifests samādhi and performs the rite of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*). Then, according to the ritual, he offers seats, argha water, and various other offerings, causing all the worthy sages to give rise to great joy. Finally, he personally performs the yoga of correspondence."
This consists of three types:
first, supplicating all Buddhas for their compassionate protection while visualizing subtle syllables transforming into the forms of Buddhas;
second, generating from one's own person the pure bodhicitta to become a Buddha of Great Wisdom.
Third, regarding the marks of the Buddha attained and those of the Bodhisattvas and others, one realizes through the Dharma that the seals (*mudrā*) are perfected.
When these three types of ritual procedures for the union of the deities are fully complete, within a single instant, miraculous transformations arise as ultimate great wisdom.

Furthermore, the practitioner, having first established themselves in samādhi, should arouse the great bodhicitta and wash away the defilements of the mind. By reciting the mantra for purifying the three karmas, the defilements of the mind become pure in a single kṣaṇa. Through the power of the mantra, one develops the bodhicitta and contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations, fundamentally empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of any solid reality.

Based on this visualization of the bodhicitta, one should conceive of it as a moon disc; upon the moon disc, one should visualize the syllable Oṃ as the Body Vajra. Next, one should visualize the syllable Āḥ as the Speech Vajra, and the syllable Hūṃ as the Mind Vajra.

Once these three syllables have thus formed the vajra body, speech, and mind, one should visualize the syllable *BHAṂ* transforming into a lotus flower. Mounted upon this lotus, one visualizes the Buddha’s body complete with all its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), having grasped the ritual procedures for the physical form and color. Then, one visualizes oneself assuming a majestic and haughty posture, thinking: "My very body is Vajratathāgata, adorned with every ornament and radiating a perfect light. This original body is itself ultimate enlightenment and great wisdom. Thereafter, according to the method of the five Tathāgatas, one uses mantras and mudrās as armor and weapons for the disciple, and immediately confers the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).

At that time, the ācārya visualizes all Buddhas filling the void and performing great miraculous transformations. He further visualizes that in each of the ten directions there is a Vidyārāja leading the fourfold army; all the Buddhas and Great Vidyārājas each bind their respective root mudrās and hold weapons in their hands, pervading the ten directions and performing various kinds of miraculous transformations.

These are the five Tathāgatas who expound the yoga of ultimate truth; through the four truths, the six perfections, and so forth—like the Karma-vajra—they perform great benefit and bring salvation to sentient beings.

"At that time, the Ācārya visualizes all Buddhas filling the void, each seated upon a lotus flower, their marks complete and adorned with every ornament. He further visualizes the Buddhas and their lotus seats merging into one; this is the non-duality of the one and the many within the Buddha-body, the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena, and the single essence of the Dharmadhātu. Thereafter, according to the ritual procedures, he presents various offerings such as playful garlands, song and dance, incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments. Alternatively, he may perform visualization; if his mind becomes weary, he should immediately engage in recitation. He must maintain right concentration with body and mind free from all distraction, neither too hurried nor too slow, ensuring the phrasing is precise and correct."

If one becomes weary from recitation, one should take up the bell and vajra, perform the offering by casting the vajra and ringing the bell according to the ritual, and then dismiss the noble deities. Thereafter, one may perform self-protection and proceed with activities as one pleases, whether walking or staying. Alternatively, if one wishes to invoke the noble deities once again, one should employ the hundred-syllable mantra.

At that time, the ācārya, visualizing and reciting according to this rite, becomes like the full moon of the heavens, neither waning nor waxing; before long, he realizes great bodhi. This person fulfills the ritual methods for the accomplishment of the Vajrayāna and likewise becomes a sovereign lord of all vidyās, just as the five families of Tathāgatas, such as Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha and the others.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, entered the *vajra-samādhi* of the accomplishment of the wisdom-wheel of all Tathāgatas. Emerging from this meditative absorption, he proclaimed the rites to be performed internally and externally for all wheels:

“The maṇḍala to be constructed according to this *Yogamahārāja-tantra* shall be named after the maṇḍala of Vajradhātu, following the name of the principal deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Thereafter, one should perform the rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and coercion (*abhicāruka*). Having visualized and recited the mantras of the principal deity and the various bodhisattvas, one should then carry out these rites.”
If one performs the rite for pacifying calamities (śāntika), one should rely upon the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā and the Bodhisattva Cundā.
If one performs the rite for increasing prosperity (pauṣṭika), one should rely upon the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhā and the Bodhisattva Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
If one performs rites for subjugation through attraction (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one should rely upon the Bodhisattvas Tārā and Vajrasaṃkalā.
If one performs rites for coercion (*abhicāra*), one should rely upon the Bodhisattvas Bhṛkuṭī and Māmakī.

"Furthermore, there are the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha and the Bodhisattva Parṇaśavarī; these two bodhisattvas are also able to eliminate calamities. If a person relies upon them to perform recitation, they will certainly attain accomplishment."
"In this way, these bodhisattvas possess great power equal to that of the Buddhas and are able to perform all rites of accomplishment.

At that time, when the practitioner wishes to perform a rite for bodily calamities, they should each visualize their own seed-syllable transforming into the Bodhisattva Locanā and the Bodhisattva Cundā, complete with all the marks and signs of perfection and every adornment. In their hands, they hold a vessel of nectar (*amṛta-kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary. With the vessel of nectar, they pour it over the crown of the head of the person afflicted by calamities and obstacles; just as one becomes naturally cooled, this can eliminate their feverish afflictions."
At that time, the practitioner of recitation should visualize himself as the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, who is fully capable of pacifying and eliminating all calamities and obstacles.
"Furthermore, perform the rite of augmentation."

At that time, the ācārya visualizes himself as the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava, with a golden-colored body, vast and perfectly complete. He further visualizes the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha and the Bodhisattva Pāṇḍaravāsinī, both likewise golden in color, holding jewels and lotuses in their hands, raining down nectar and precious gems, capable of performing the supreme rite of increase (puṣṭi).
"Furthermore, regarding the rite for creating affection:

the practitioner should visualize Amitāyus Buddha, whose physical form is red in color, vast and perfectly complete. One should further visualize the Bodhisattva Tārā and the Bodhisattva Vajraśṛṅkhalā, both of whom are also red in color and hold nooses and vajra-hooks in their hands. To cause others to feel affection, one uses these hooks and nooses to draw them in."
In this way, according to the ritual, one will swiftly attain the power of attraction.
Furthermore, for the rite of pacification (*śāntika*):
the reciter should visualize the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha and the Bodhisattva Parṇaśavarī filling the entirety of space and raining down nectar; thus, calamities and obstacles will be eliminated.
"Furthermore, regarding the method for subjugation:

The practitioner first visualizes the syllable HŪṂ transforming into the Buddha Amoghasiddhi, whose body is green in color, vast and perfectly complete. He further visualizes the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī and the Bodhisattva Māmakī, their bodies green in color, with vajra-light radiating from their entire forms, manifesting in a state of great wrath. They rain down the great fire of the gods to burn the body of the person being subjugated, creating a state of terror."
When one contemplates the dharmas in this manner, within a single kṣaṇa, the bodies of those beings who have been subdued will be damaged and even utterly extinguished.
"Furthermore, the four Bodhisattvas, such as Sattvavajra and the others, are able to perform the empowerment rite for sentient beings."
Furthermore, there are sixteen great bodhisattvas who are able to perform all methods of accomplishment within the supreme maṇḍala.
Additionally, there are various vidyārājas who, through visualization according to the ritual rules, are able to perform methods of subjugation.
"Furthermore, perform the rite of external subjugation.
The practitioner should take earth from beneath the feet of the person to be subdued, earth from both banks of a river, funeral ashes, and clothing from a corpse;
mixing these with *khaḷamuṇḍara* to form a clay paste, he should fashion an image of the person to be subdued. Furthermore, using..."
Having mixed mustard seeds, poison, salt, and *mimuttra*, and smeared them upon the body of that image, one should visualize that the image’s mind becomes agitated;
it is blown by the wind into the sky, where it is hooked with a vajra-hook and bound with a lasso.
Reciting the name of the person to be subdued, one strikes it with a bone-mallet.

Prick his entire body with thorns, and further, using human bone pegs or *khadira* wood pegs, nail them into five locations on the effigy of the one to be subdued—namely, the head, forehead, arms, heart, and neck.
Then, using a sharp sword, cut it off from the feet. Having kindled a fire with *nimba* wood fuel, [proceed as follows].
Manifesting the form of a great wrathful deity, one should perform homa within that fire using the severed image.
When this rite is performed—whether at midnight or at midday—even the power of the Buddhas and noble ones cannot save the person being subdued, let alone the gods who might protect them.
"Furthermore, perform the rite of internal subjugation. According to the ritual rules, the practitioner first removes the protective charms of the person to be subdued.

Then, visualize the various Vidyārājas manifesting in wrathful forms, each holding a sword, staff, vajra, pestle, noose, wheel, bow, arrow, and so forth. With the noose of the Vidyārāja, bind the person to be subdued and lead them toward the south. Along the way, another Vidyārāja strikes them with a vajra to terrify them. Immediately, open that person's abdomen with a sharp sword and extract their intestines and stomach. Then, recite this mantra of the Vidyārāja:"

"Oṃ hūṃ vajrarākṣasa bhañja bhañja. Having recited this mantra, one should further visualize that the hosts of Vajra-rākṣasas transform into crows, foxes, vultures, and the like, all gathering together to devour the person being subdued. One should further visualize that person riding upon a camel, traveling southward atop a wind-wheel, while the Vidyārāja follows behind, striking and hurling [objects] at him.
By visualizing in this manner, that person who seeks to subjugate one will swiftly be eliminated.
"Furthermore, regarding the method for exorcism:

the practitioner, relying on the ritual of union with Vajraśūṇḍa, takes a leaf blown by a whirlwind and inscribes upon it the mantra as well as the name of the person to be exorcised. Then, taking earth from beneath that person's feet, he places it together with the inscribed leaf and treads upon them with his foot while reciting the mantra of the Honored One. Thus, the exorcism is swiftly accomplished; even Śakra, Lord of Devas, cannot protect [the offender], let alone ordinary mortals."
"Furthermore, regarding the method for exorcism:

the practitioner shall take the wing of a *śṛgāla* (jackal), inscribe upon it the mantra and the name of the person to be subdued, and wrap it with the hair of a Brahmin of pure conduct. He should then recite the mantra while consecrating it and bury it secretly in the ground. Furthermore, he should visualize two Great Vidyārājas striking that person; next, he should visualize the syllable *HŪṂ* transforming into a minute vajra which enters the body of the person to be subdued, becoming a *karmavajra*. With great blazing flames, it strikes that person, causing all their limbs and joints to wither away. He should further visualize various Vajra-Ḍākinīs all coming to devour the blood from the body of the person to be subdued."
By performing the ritual in this manner, one will swiftly achieve expulsion. Recite this mantra:

"Oṃ vajranarkiṇi amukasya rakṣata-ākarṣaya hūṃ phaṭ. Having recited this mantra, if one acts in accordance with the dharma, that person to be subdued will quickly have their limbs wither away and even be utterly destroyed.
"Furthermore, regarding the rite for causing rain:

the practitioner proceeds to the northwest corner; having smeared a four-sided maṇḍala with scented water, he applies seven dots of fragrant ointment in the shape of stars and covers them with a clean vessel."

The practitioner visualizes the seven points of fragrant paste of the maṇḍala as an eight-sided Mount Sumeru, which transforms into vajras that completely fill the surrounding space; he then further visualizes the syllable *ya* becoming a great wind-wheel, tranquil and motionless.
In this manner, by relying on the ritual, one is able to cause great rain to fall.
Furthermore, regarding the method for causing rain:

the reciter should visualize eight great nāga kings upon an eight-petaled lotus flower—namely, the nāga king Ānanda, the nāga king Kūlika, the nāga king Vāsuki, the nāga king Takṣaka, the nāga king Mahāpadma, the nāga king Karkoṭaka, the nāga king Śaṅkhapāla, and the nāga king Padma. These are the nāga kings.

In this manner, each of the nāga kings, having visualized their respective forms, ornaments, and implements according to the ritual rules, proceeds at night to a crossroads. There, using scented water, they smear the four directions of the maṇḍala with the left thumb and draw vajra-hooks and other symbols within the four corners.
At that time, the practitioner shall arrange a seat before the maṇḍala and sit down; furthermore, they should visualize and recite the mantras of the eight great nāga kings together with their names.
By practicing in this manner according to the ritual, one will be able to bring down heavy rain.
"Furthermore, regarding the ritual for causing rain:

the reciter should visualize eight great nāga kings upon the previously mentioned eight-petaled lotus. At the center of the lotus is the Great Fierce Wrathful Vidyārāja, whose bodily radiance is blazing and fierce, manifesting as a garuḍa that drives the nāgas away."
At that time, the practitioner should recite the syllables *huṃ huṃ* and the mantra of the Nāga King.
By thus visualizing and reciting, a great rain will surely fall.
Furthermore, the method for stopping the rain:

The reciter visualizes himself as the fire of samādhi. From between his eyebrows, he emanates the Vidyārāja Acala, whose entire body blazes with light like the sun. He is also like the body of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, possessing six arms: the right hands hold a sword, a vajra, and an arrow; the left hands hold a wheel, a noose, and a bow. Furthermore, he visualizes the emanation of various vidyārājas and rain-like showers of wheels, swords, nooses, bows, arrows, and vajras filling the sky, and then recites the root mantra.
When one acts in accordance with the Dharma in this manner, the heavy rain will immediately cease and the terrors of Māra will be dispelled.
Furthermore, regarding the method for removing the alarm and terror caused by Māra:

the practitioner should mix *nararudira* (human flesh) with clean earth to fashion an image of the Māra-foe. Having done so, they should recite the Kilana-mantra twenty-one times. Then, according to the ritual of the Bodhisattva from the previous day, they should visualize Pināyaka entering the mouth of the subduing deity and strike him with a pestle, while reciting the Gada-mantra as follows:
"Oṃ saṃbhava-vajra-muśalīna-cūḍāya nāraviṇa hūṃ phaṭ. By reciting this according to the ritual method, within a single kṣaṇa, the māras will themselves become terrified, retreat, and flee.
"Furthermore, regarding the rite for bringing down rain:

the practitioner should visualize Śakra as having three faces and four arms, with a body the color of the moon. He rides upon a white elephant with eight bodies and a thousand heads; this elephant has a thousand eyes and a thousand tusks. His right hand holds a vajra, and his left hand holds a bell resting at his waist. His physical form is perfect, manifesting the appearance of great magnificence, surrounded in mid-air by four celestial maidens, bringing benefit and joy to sentient beings."
Desiring to bring down sweet rain, one should address the nāgas, saying:
"May you quickly send down rain.
Furthermore, one should visualize the garuḍa pressing upon the nāga kings, pecking at them with its beak to cause them to send down sweet rain, and then recite this mantra as follows:
“Oṃ vajranārāyaṇa niriṣyapa vahe nimamamekha hūṃ. Having recited this mantra, a great rain will descend immediately, like water pouring from a jar.
"Furthermore, the mantra is as follows:

'Oṃ mahāsukhavajra ṭiṃ hūṃ. The practitioner, reciting this mantra, performs the vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*) and visualizes according to the ritual procedure; thus they will be able to accomplish matters of supreme benefit and bliss."

At that time, after the Bhagavān Mahāvairocana Vajra Tathāgata had taught this subtle and true dharma of mantra-visualization, his heart was filled with great joy. Looking upon the great assembly, and in order to subdue all beings through great wisdom, he held the vajra and entered the samādhi of Great Bliss.

Having emerged from meditative absorption, because he brings forth great wisdom through skillful means, he places his two hands like lotuses upon his crown; from between his own eyebrows, he emits a great radiance, manifesting the signs of the three secrets of body, speech, and mind.

At that time, Akṣobhya Buddha, Ratnasambhava Buddha, Amitāyus Buddha, Amoghasiddhi Buddha, along with the sixteen great bodhisattvas, and even all the vidyārājas, entered the profound dharma-gate and attained mastery in samādhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions has this great radiance been emitted to universally illuminate the entire assembly?”
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana Vajra uttered a great and wondrous voice and addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."
This luminous sign is revealed in the subtle dharma-gate of profound and secret visualization; it brings great benefit and joy, accomplishing vajra great wisdom and realizing the path to bodhi.
And he spoke in verse:
"The reality-mark of bodhi is neither existent nor non-existent; It is without the two extremes and no middle way.
Free from marks, quiescent, and like space— What is there for the Buddhas of the three times to realize?"
Now I shall explain the subtle and wondrous great skillful means, Causing them to awaken to and enter the bodhicitta;
With wisdom free from grasping and rejecting, one contemplates the aggregates, Revealing only the mind of the Great Way of True Emptiness.
The Tathāgata of supreme excellence is the Buddha of the three bodies; True mind is not found within the body.
All dharmas arise from the mind; The dharmas thus produced are themselves bodhi.
Just as a magician, with a mind of illusion, Produces various kinds of illusory transformations, So too do all these arise from false conceptualization;
The characteristics of the bodhicitta are likewise thus.
The Great Wisdom of Vajra arises from the mind, skillfully acting as the cause for unsurpassed bodhi;
when afflictions and doubts defile that mind, it teaches in accordance with the faculties and natures of sentient beings.
I see that fools distinguish between defilement and purity, Failing to realize that this body is a mere provisional union of the four elements.
By contemplating the unconditioned true nature as empty, One ultimately accomplishes great Bodhi.
At that time, after the Great Vairocana Vajra Tathāgata had spoken these verses, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Such is the nature of bodhi, which is inherently pure and possesses two meanings:
first, it is not the arising of afflictions, because the aggregates have no reality."
2. Its nature is like space because it is beyond the reach of conceptual thought.
This true bodhi is what all Buddhas proclaim; if a person contemplates it, they will immediately abide in great wisdom and be able to perform the rites for the accomplishment of *karma*.
The Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva:

“If there are those who uphold and recite [this mantra] and constantly practice the methods for accomplishment, yet despite diligent seeking find it ultimately difficult to achieve success, I shall now explain for you the method of subjugation, through which one may swiftly attain accomplishment by means of the skillful means of Great Bliss.”

The practitioner should rely upon the rite of the Great Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśa; the Vajrapāśa possesses great power, the Vajramuṣṭi is exceedingly fierce and sharp, the Vajrakīla can destroy, the Vajraghaṇṭā can strike, and the Vajragaḷī-mudrā is greatly courageous—when all such deities behold these, they are utterly terrified.

This is the samādhi of the Buddha. If a practitioner recites according to the ritual and visualizes accordingly, reciting the syllable HŪṂ, they will emit a vajra hook that skillfully enters the hearts of all Buddhas; seeing this samādhi, they will all swiftly arrive. This method can summon all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, let alone ordinary sentient beings.

At that time, when the practitioner of recitation seeks accomplishment by performing this rite of subjugation, they should visualize binding [the opponent] with the vajra-bind. They should form the threatening gesture with the vajra-kāli mudrā and strike with the vajra-solid fist. Furthermore, they should nail the five locations—the crown of the head, the forehead, the neck, the heart, and the arms—with vajra-pestles, using vajra-impaling stakes to drive them in.

By practicing in accordance with this method, even the most malevolent demons and adversaries will swiftly submit themselves; the supreme accomplishment will certainly be perfected, and the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi will be realized before long.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the entire great assembly, having heard this secret method of accomplishment through union, were filled with great joy and praised it with one voice, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
“World-Honored One!
This Great Union is secret, profound, firm, and far-reaching; it is able to analyze and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings.
Then he spoke in verse:
“Excellent, O Unsurpassed One, Great Fearless One, All-Illuminating Vajra Great Tathāgata!
You have well expounded the true and subtle Dharma, Benefiting all sentient beings.”
The Great Power Vajra Purification Hook can enter the hearts of all Buddhas of Great Wisdom;
it accomplishes the supreme vehicle of the Vajra and penetrates the secret, unconditioned mark.
If a person practices diligently according to this Dharma, they will before long fully realize the fruit of Bodhi.
At that time, after Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others had spoken these verses, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra immediately spoke the mantras of the Vajrāṅkuśa and the others:

“Oṃ vajrākarṣaya hūṃ | Oṃ vajrapāśa bandha hūṃ | Oṃ vajrāṅkuśi tarjaya hūṃ | Oṃ vajramuṣṭi gṛhṇa phaṭ hūṃ | These mantras of the Vajra Hook and others are pure, subtle, and possess great power; they bring benefit to immeasurable beings. If one recites them according to the ritual, there is nothing that will not be accomplished.”
It is the most supreme among the great wisdoms of the Vajra; it must not be transmitted to those with wrong views or other such unrighteous persons. Chapter Nine:

The Homa Ritual The Buddha Speaks the King of Great Yoga Teachings Sūtra, Chapter Nine: The Homa Ritual. At that time, the Bhagavān, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, again entered the vajra-samādhi corresponding to the performance of the ritual procedures for all accomplishments. Emerging from that concentration, he spoke the *prabodhana-siddhi* (the method of awakening):

“At that time, the practitioner of recitation should first visualize the syllable Oṃ at the crown of his head, the syllable A in his mouth, and the syllable Hūṃ in his heart. He should further visualize the syllable Va transforming into a wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Upon this wheel is the one who awakens, capable of explaining all matters of the world.”
The practitioner assumes a majestic and haughty posture, then visualizes the Bodhisattva Cundā and recites the Cundā Bodhisattva mantra as follows:
*Namo sabhdata-nam samyak-sambuddha-kuṭi-nam* (Namo sabhdata-nam samyak-sambuddha-kuṭi-nam) (Note:
*Sabhdata* is a transliteration of *sadbhūta*; *nam* is *namaḥ*; *samyak-sambuddha* is *samyaksambuddha*; *kuṭi* is *kūṭi*).

*Sarve śāntya svāhā.* (83) At that time, when the Ācārya recites this mantra, he should hold a vajra, shake a vajra-bell, and form the vajra-bandha mudrā, moving it back and forth. Next, he should visualize the syllable *Oṃ* transforming into a Maheśvara maṇḍala. He should further visualize an eight-petaled lotus within the maṇḍala, with the syllable *A* upon each petal, and four *Hūṃ* syllables at the center of the lotus. Covering these with two vessels, he should visualize within the maṇḍala the Principal Deity subduing that person. Then, he should recite the root mantra and further visualize the syllable *Vaṃ* as a protective boundary.
By visualizing and reciting in this manner, one can bind all sentient beings, including even gods and humans.
Furthermore, I shall now explain the ritual for accomplishing *homa*.
The Fire Deity presides over all the deities, and they all constantly abide in the reality of homa, skillfully performing various activities.

This homa can sacrifice to all the deities and bring about all accomplishments (*siddhi*). If a practitioner’s recitation lacks syllables or their ritual procedures are incomplete, by performing this homa, everything becomes perfected; for this reason, the Buddhas of the three periods and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions all praise the method of homa.

If one wishes to perform the three types of homa—śāntika (pacification), pauṣṭika (augmentation), and vaśya (subjugation)—one should produce fire by drilling wood. If performing homa for tasks such as abhicāra (destruction), one should use fire from the house of a caṇḍāla or fire from within a śmaśāna (cremation ground).
This homa fire-pit has four types of forms:
first, the form of a full moon; second, the form of a half-moon;
[third, the form of a triangle; fourth, the form of a square].
Third, the square-shaped; fourth, the triangular-shaped. Each of these four types of hearths has its own *homa* mudrā method.

Within the hearth, one should place the symbols of the wheel, vajra, jewel, lotus, and so forth. Outside the *homa* hearth, one should install the insignia according to the ritual rules. To the right of the hearth, one should place the *pātrī-sruva* ladle and all other necessary items. One should spread *śamī* grass (auspicious grass) all around the perimeter. To the left of the hearth, one should place the *argha* water bowl. Reciting the *Sarvasiddhi-mantra*, one consecrates the *argha* water and purifies one’s own hands. Then, according to the ritual rules, one kindles the firewood and invokes the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*), reciting this invocation mantra as follows:

"Vahana-ya svāhā. The practitioner recites this mantra, joins the palms of both hands, and after moving the right thumb, uses *argha* water to lightly sprinkle and purify the interior of the fire with the left hand, then immediately performs the five subtle offerings.

Visualize that the Fire Deity (Agni) descends from the southeast corner: his body is short and his belly is large; his entire body is crimson in color; he has four arms and four faces, each with three eyes; he wears a jeweled crown upon his head with his hair tied in a topknot; he sits upon a wheel of fire, his entire body radiating *karma*-light; his first right hand forms the *varada-mudrā* (gesture of granting boons), his second right hand holds a rosary; his first left hand holds a water jar (*kundikā*), and his second left hand holds a staff; his body is adorned with various jewels, and he is surrounded by a retinue of celestial beings.
Having performed this visualization, one then invites the Fire Deity (Agni) to enter the homa furnace.

At that time, the ācārya performs the homa by casting the homa substances into the furnace three times. Having purified his hands with arghya water and presented the offerings, he dedicates the merit to express gratitude to the Fire Deity and announces the specific rite he wishes to accomplish. Thereafter, he discerns the auspicious or inauspicious signs of the homa flames.
If the flames are white, or shaped like a parasol or a banner, or resemble an *argha* vessel turning clockwise, these are all auspicious signs that the fundamental rite will be accomplished.

When the *ācārya* beholds such auspicious signs, he should immediately recite sublime songs of praise; while reciting these praises, beginning with the syllable *Oṃ* and ending with the syllable *Svāhā*, his Brahma-voice should be continuous, resonant, and melodious. Thus, the rite will certainly be accomplished.

If performing the rite of pacification (*śāntika*), one should give rise to a mind of compassion; if performing the rite of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), one should give rise to a firm and non-retrogressive mind; if performing the rite of magnetizing (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one should give rise to a mind of reverence and love; if performing the rite of subjugation (*abhicāruka*), one should manifest a wrathful appearance and give rise to a mind that devours the three realms.

In this manner, each ācārya, according to the respective dharma, should recite the mantra-texts of their own specific family with perfect accuracy, present various kinds of extensive offerings, and be fully conversant with all aspects of the homa ritual.
If performing a homa, first perform the homa with a full *pātra* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and thereafter proceed according to the sequence of the ritual rules.
If performing the three types of rites—pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*paustika*), and subjugation (*vaśya*)—one should perform the homa using auspicious and wholesome substances;
if performing the rite of coercion (*abhicāra*), one should perform the homa using fierce and inauspicious substances.

"Such is the secret dharma of yoga; it opens the gate of visualization to enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the essential and sublime path for bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
He then spoke in verse:
"All ignorant and deluded sentient beings, With stubborn hearts, commit manifold evils."
If such sinful karma is thus accomplished, how can one obtain virtuous fruit?
Those who are deluded and ignorant lack the wisdom of skillful means;
regarding this secret gate, they turn their backs on it and fail to practice it.
Deeply attached to external objects, they give rise to deluded thoughts and ignorance,
making no distinction between sin and merit.
That there is neither arising nor ceasing is the skillful means taught by the Buddha.
To purify the wisdom of sentient beings,
as well as those [afflictions] like rivers and so forth, one must rely upon a boat or raft to be able to reach the other shore.
In the difficulty of being swept away and drowned by the four currents, one must board the boat of the practice of the Dharma to reach the shore of Bodhi.
One achieves the profound Dharma, the path taught by the Tathāgata.
Do not harbor doubts, nor disparage and fail to accept this;
otherwise, you will sink into the ocean of birth and death, with no time of liberation.
Remain tranquil in body and mind, and stay far removed from the defilement of delusions.
Through the union of body, speech, and mind, One gives birth to the wisdom of skillful means;
By severing the notions of self and person, One realizes all-knowledge through direct manifestation.

Chapter Ten: Entrustment The Yoga Mahātantrarāja Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Chapter Ten: Entrustment At that time, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana Vajra entered the samādhi of the Supreme Accomplishment Vajra. Emerging from that meditative absorption, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
“Listen attentively! I shall now explain the method for accomplishing the supreme Great Samaya within all samādhis, known as the Vajra.

Through these secret accomplishment mantras, meditative visualizations, and corresponding ritual procedures, one will be well able to accomplish the vajra body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, never to regress.”

"Furthermore, having placed the wheel before the Ācārya and recited the root mantra, he enters the samādhi of the Tathāgata Vairocana. By the power of this recitation and the majesty of the samādhi, the sacred wheel is immediately accomplished; it rises from the ground with blazing radiance. Then, reciting the mantra of the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā and holding the wheel in his hand, in an instant he transforms himself into the Tathāgata Vairocana without distinction, turning the Great Wheel of Dharma to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings, causing them to attain entry into the noble paths of the Three Vehicles."
"Furthermore, having placed a vajra before the ācārya and recited the root mantra, he enters the samādhi of Akṣobhya Tathāgata."

By the power of this recitation and samādhi, it immediately becomes a sacred vajra; rising from the earth with blazing radiance, as soon as one holds the vajra in hand, one’s own body transforms into that of Akṣobhya Tathāgata without distinction, surrounded by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Wielding the Vajra, one traverses the triple world and dwells within the hearts of all sentient beings, bestowing their aspirations upon them.
"Furthermore, having placed a jewel before the Ācārya and recited the root mantra, he enters the *samādhi* of the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava.

By the power of the recitation and the majesty of the *samādhi*, it immediately becomes a sacred jewel; rising from the ground, it blazes with intense light. He then recites the mantra of the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha and, holding the jewel-light in his hand, illuminates the ten directions. He then transforms his own body into that of the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava without distinction, wielding a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) as he travels through Buddha-fields, raining down great jewels to eliminate the suffering of poverty for all sentient beings."
"Furthermore, having placed a lotus flower before the ācārya and recited the root mantra, he enters the samādhi of the Tathāgata Amitāyus."

Through the power of the majesty of mantra-recitation and samādhi, the sacred flower is immediately formed; it rises from the earth with blazing radiance. One then recites the mantra of the Bodhisattva Pāṇḍaravāsinī while holding the flower in hand. Thereupon, one transforms oneself into the Buddha Amitāyus without any difference, dwelling in the world of Sukhāvatī, with a face like the full moon, holding the Dharma-nectar to bestow it upon all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, having placed a precious sword before the ācārya and recited the root mantra, he enters the samādhi of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi."

Through the power of the majesty of mantra-recitation and samādhi, it immediately becomes a sacred sword; rising from the earth with blazing radiance, one recites the mantra of Bodhisattva Tārā while holding the sword in hand. Thereupon, one transforms one’s own body into no different from the Buddha Amoghasiddhi, cool as the moon, traveling through the buddha-fields to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings and eliminate their afflictions.
"In this way, by relying on the teachings to maintain and recite these five kinds of noble dharmas, such as the wheels and so forth, one shall attain accomplishment.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana-vajra, entered the Vajra-samādhi of Abiding in Equality; having emerged from that meditative absorption, he gazed upon the great assembly and remained silent.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in homage to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If there is an ācārya who has received empowerment within this Great Yoga Teaching of the Secrets of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, how should the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas regard him?"
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!
Those Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas regard this consecrated Ācārya as they regard the true mind of bodhi, without any duality.”
"Why is this? Because the rite of consecration and bodhi are one.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! Listen attentively now.

All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who are currently preaching the Dharma come to the place of this ācārya three times each day to present great offerings, no different from those made to the Buddha himself, and they all raise their voices in unison, saying:”
"This Ācārya is our parents, as well as our teachers, we Buddhas.
Furthermore, son of good family!

The immeasurable merit accumulated through the three karmas of all those Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who currently reside and teach the Dharma in all the worlds of the ten directions—this is equal to the merit within a single pore of such an Ācārya.
Why is this? Because this ācārya, having received the yoga initiation, is in accord with the wisdom of all Buddhas; his true mind is subtle and wondrous, being without equal.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the Bodhisattva Maitreya marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and stood before the Buddha.

Then, the Tathāgatas Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitāyus, Amoghasiddhi, and Mahāvairocana entered the Vajra-samādhi characterized by the samaya of the Vajrācārya. Emerging from that meditative absorption, they addressed the Tathāgatas and those Bodhisattvas, saying:
“Listen attentively! Listen attentively!”
All Buddhas of the three times come to the place of the ācārya to pay homage and make offerings. Why is this?
This Vajra-ācārya is the Lord of Wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, those Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, having heard what the Buddha had said, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Upon what should the methods for accomplishing the three secrets of the vajra body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas rely?”
The Buddha said:
"The methods for accomplishing the three secrets of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas should be maintained according to the body, speech, and mind of the Vajrācārya."
Furthermore, the bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Upon what should the body, speech, and mind of this Vajrācārya rely for their abiding?"
The Buddha said:
"One should dwell in reliance upon empty space.
The Bodhisattva addressed him, saying:
“Upon what should space abide?
The Buddha said:
“It abides upon the mind of the Vajrācārya.”
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Upon what does the mind depend for its abiding?
The Buddha said:
“The mind is fundamentally detached from characteristics and has no place of abiding.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the bodhisattvas and others marveled at its rarity and remained silent.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"In this Great Teaching of Yoga, there are ten kinds of secret and true meanings:
first, the maṇḍala;..."
2. Samādhi; 3. Mudrā; 4. Gait.
Five, the seating posture;
six, the recitation;
seven, the homa fire ritual;
8. Worship; 9. Past Deeds; 10. Correspondence.
These ten dharmas arise from great wisdom; they are profoundly secret and have been proclaimed together by all the Buddhas of the three times.

If disciples who study these teachings and those who have received empowerment constantly practice respect, honor, and offerings toward their ācārya, they shall receive and uphold the instructions of the three mysteries and yogas according to their own capacities and in accordance with the Dharma, transmitting them from one to another to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.
The Buddha said:
"You, O Ācāryas and others, must not transmit this Great Yoga Tantra to those who lack the faculty of faith, nor to the foolish who disparage the Dharma."
If one transmits this to them, the Dharma will not be accomplished and their samādhi will be destroyed; at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into the great hells.

Furthermore, if there are those who do not rely on this sublime Dharma, the nectar of immortality, to apply themselves with diligence and practice, such persons cannot sever all afflictions, let alone perform various ascetic practices by sacrificing their heads, eyes, hands, feet, and other limbs.

If a person, within this teaching, practices even a single dharma or a single conduct with diligent mastery through recitation, abides in tranquility, and enters samādhi, they will be able to sever the afflictions and directly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bodhisattvas and the assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
